subsubtopic: MADE BY PRIME MINISTER IN CUBA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the terms of Standing Order 43 to seek leave to propose a motion arising out of remarks attributed to the Prime Minister in Cuba yesterday which are in many ways reminiscent of the 1967 incident involving President de Gaulle's "Vive Quebec Libre". I would move, seconded by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley:
With reference to yesterday's declarations and outbursts of "Viva" by the Prime Minister in Cuba, the House considers these, especially at a time when Cuba is heavily involved militarily in the Angolan civil war, a deplorable, degrading and disgusting incident which will undoubtedly and unfortunately be construed by world opinion as indicating Canada's support for dictatorial socialism, and, finally, the House dissociates itself from all recent utterances of the Prime Minister indicating disapproval of the free enterprise system.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF FACILITIES FOR SPECTATORS AND ATHLETES- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. It is prompted by today's report that the Olympic Games stadium will not provide for flush toilets for some 70,000 spectators or proper changing facilities for some 10,000 athletes. I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez):
That the Minister of the Environment be requested to impose standards under the Clean Air Act and the new Environmental Contaminants Act which forbids, in section 2, "spilling, leaking, spraying, pouring, emitting, emptying, throwing or dumping of dangerous substances into the environment" and that the Minister of National Health and Welfare be requested to provide curtains for those athletes changing in their cars so that proper standards of modesty can be maintained and, third, that in view of past disappointments and future uncertainties in the construction of the Olympic site the Minister of Public Works obtain assurances for the House that the Games Committee will provide 70,000 one-holers rather than one 70,000-holer.

subtopic: SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF DANGER OF MERCURY POISONING IN NORTHWEST QUEBEC-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that a report from Environment Canada has clearly shown that an industry in the Matagami and Lebel-sur-Quevillon area is a major source of mercury pollution and considering that such a source is liable to cause serious diseases among all individuals contaminated by mercury, I move, seconded by the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs investigate the dangers of mercury poisoning on the spot in Northwestern Quebec and report to this House on the means to be taken to protect the people of Northwestern Quebec from the serious danger of mercury poisoning.

That this House instruct the Minister of Finance to introduce immediately amendments to the anti-inflation legislation guaranteeing the prompt establishment of a just, non-arbitrary and equitable appeals procedure from Anti-Inflation Board decisions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43 and ask for the unanimous consent of the House; I am sure that no hon. member can disagree with such a motion.
Considering that almost half of the colour TV sets sold in Canada, that is 46 per cent, are manufactured outside Canada, mostly in Japan and in the United States, and that the importation of such colour TV sets is detrimental to Canada and Quebec manufacturers and workers; and considering also that the Fleetwood company, the only colour TV manufacturer in Quebec, just said that it has to dismiss 150 employees, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House immediately take the required steps to exercise stricter control over U.S. and Asian importations in order to give greater protection to Canada and, particularly Quebec workers, where the unemployment rate is rising alarmingly.

subsubtopic: EMISSION LEVELS AT SYNCRUDE-POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF FEDERAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I received a letter yesterday in reply to questions I put to the Minister of the Environment concerning environmental controls in respect of the Syncrude project, in which the minister stated at one point that his department intends to use the "best practicable technology". Since the minister's own departmental study in 1974 on the Syncrude project indicated that it was possible to reduce the level of emission of sulphur dioxide to 40 long tons per day, why has this department permitted the project to proceed with levels of emission which will reach up to 287 long tons a day?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: EMISSION LEVELS AT SYNCRUDE-POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF FEDERAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first responsibility in that field lies, of course, with the government of Alberta. We have made some studies and my department believes it is possible to reduce the amount of sulphur dioxide emission from 287 long tons a day to 40 long tons a day. That being possible, the government is pressing the companies to use this new technology in order to obtain this reduction.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: EMISSION LEVELS AT SYNCRUDE-POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF FEDERAL STANDARDS
speechtext: In the minister's letter to me he has indicated that the government has entered into an agreement with the government of Alberta that will permit "levels of emission up to the level of 287 long tons". What the minister is now saying, if I understand him well, is that this might not be the case, and that it is possible to get a level of control which is more rigorous than this, a level this government wants. What I want to do is get this minister, who is responsible for the environment in Canada, to make a commitment that it is the objective of this government, which holds an equity in the Syncrude project and is on the management committee, to insist on this standard as a condition to further federal participation.

subsubtopic: EMISSION LEVELS AT SYNCRUDE-POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF FEDERAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. gentleman that I will insist on having this present emission reduced. While it is true that we hold equity in the Syncrude project it is a small percentage, I think about 15 per cent, but even without a majority of the shares we intend to exercise pressure on these companies to do this.

subsubtopic: EMISSION LEVELS AT SYNCRUDE-POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF FEDERAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to be as precise as possible on this matter. I would ask the minister whether the government is going to insist that the project comply with these possibilities indicated in the department's own study of 1974? Is the government going to insist that these practicable levels, a phrase which the minister used in his letter to me, are to be complied with in Syncrude as a condition to continued future federal government participation?

subsubtopic: EMISSION LEVELS AT SYNCRUDE-POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF FEDERAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are going to advise the department of energy, as we have already done, in respect of this matter, as Syncrude does not come under my jurisdiction. I think what the hon. member suggests is something the department of energy is ready to do. I am sure the minister can answer for that department. As far as I am concerned, I am going to continue to advise, as in the past, that the Syncrude project should comply with these new standards.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION AGAINST ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Justice.
Considering that Quebec's commission against organized crime is, in the eyes of the people, a dismal farce whose only contribution has been to release the names of members of the underworld and murderers, can the minister tell us whether or not federal justice will step in, as some of those known criminals are let loose in the city of Montreal and no one seems to do anything about it while decent citizens are left at their mercy? Will federal authorities eventually intervene in the commission's activities?

January 29, 1976
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I think the inquiry that has been held in Quebec has exposed a number of people, some of whom have been charged under federal or provincial statutes. If there is evidence in the hands of the crown attorneys of the province of Quebec, I am confident that that evidence would be used to bring charges against persons in respect of whom they have evidence.

QUEBEC CRIME PROBE-GOVERNMENT ACTION IF COMMISSION DECLARED UNCONSTITUTIONAL

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON LIMITATION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address my question to the Minister of Labour. I wonder whether the minister would indicate to the House if the government has changed its policy in the area of industrial disputes in favour of free collective bargaining as opposed to a policy of limitation of right to strike in so-called essential services or with respect to trade unions that possibly are so strong they can make unfair demands on employers. Has that policy been changed or is it the same policy as indicated by the Prime Minister prior to Christmas?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON LIMITATION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure that I fully understand the question put by the hon. member, but at any rate let me say that our policy with respect to free collective bargaining is the same as it has always been. What we are endeavouring to do, however, is to arrive at better techniques through consultation with management and labour on an active basis through the mechanism of the tripartite council, the Canada Labour Relations Council.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON LIMITATION OF RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext: I wonder if I may ask the Minister of Labour if this policy has not been changed whether the Minister of Transport was expressing government policy when he indicated that he supported the elimination of the strike weapon in cases where unions are able to make excessive wage demands on employers, and that such measures should not only apply to so-called essential services, or is the government reviewing the whole question of the right to strike and, if so, can we expect legislation in this area in the near future?

subtopic: PROPOSED INFORMATION PROGRAM TO MAINTAIN MARKETS IN UNITED STATES
PROPOSED INFORMATION PROGRAM TO MAINTAIN MARKETS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Has he been made aware and has he studied the recently issued report of our Senate Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs which states the following:
Canada must set up an improved information program in the United States, or risk jeopardizing its trade with the United States market.
Has the minister examined that report and, if so, does he or his department intend to take steps to overcome this serious deficiency in promoting trade with our most important customer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROPOSED INFORMATION PROGRAM TO MAINTAIN MARKETS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not read the report in full but I have been briefed by the chairman and the senators concerned. I am inclined to agree very much that we must step up our efforts to make the Canadian position, and Canada, generally better known in the United States. I think the hon. member will agree that I could not act more rapidly. The new minister of commerce will be sworn in on Monday. My request to him to see me will be filled as soon as he is sworn in. The new United States ambassador to Canada is being received, I believe, on the 17th of next month and I have an appointment with him on the 18th. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR REGULATIONS CONCERNING BLUE TONGUE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question relating to the livestock disease known as blue tongue and I wish to address it to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the very irresponsible lead editorial in the January issue of American Hereford Journal concerning Canada's new health of animals requirement for double testing for the blue tongue disease in imported cattle, and notwithstanding the need and validity of this new Canadian regulation for the protection of Canada's global trade relations in cattle, beef and sheep, would the minister consider making a formal statement giving the essential facts and reasons for Canada's revised policy regarding blue tongue?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR REGULATIONS CONCERNING BLUE TONGUE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I think it should be said here that Canada is free of this disease, both in the cattle population and the sheep population, and it is most important that we keep that record. I understand today that the U.S. secretary of state for agriculture has informed cattlemen in his country that he would do the same thing to protect his cattle industry if it was in the position in which the Canadian cattle industry finds itself.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR REGULATIONS CONCERNING BLUE TONGUE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: In view of the likelihood of imminent public reaction in the United States demanding retaliatory action calling for similar testing procedures on Canadian cattle and possibly other border state actions, would the minister not feel it would be appropriate to further discuss this matter with U.S. Secretary Butz in view of the very real possibility that U.S. action could very well damage and impair the recent return to normal cattle trading practice between our two countries following the abolition of the quotas?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR REGULATIONS CONCERNING BLUE TONGUE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: We are very concerned about any action which may be taken by the United States, but we have had discussions with U.S. department of agriculture officials. They are fully informed about our concern with respect to our livestock being free from this disease, and we will be discussing it further with them to make sure people in their country who are concerned about this disease are fully informed and understand our position. When I was in the United States we did discuss blue tongue. The largest cattle population is in the state of Texas, and they are having difficulty in the state of Texas trying to control this disease. The only way to control it is to eradicate it. We have had to eradicate several herds imported from the United States in recent months because of blue tongue disease.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. In view of the fact that, as I informed him, some 25 per cent to 28 per cent of the labour force of 44,000 now in industrial Cape Breton is currently unemployed, and that the premier of Nova Scotia called a special meeting on January 19 to be followed by another meeting on February 9, at which the minister had a representative present, I should like to ask the minister if he would inform the House what projects or financial involvement may be forthcoming from the federal government to help alleviate this crisis situation in the short term and medium term development for the Cape Breton area.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am fully aware of the distressingly high unemployment rate in Cape Breton, and I am also aware that it may increase for a number of reasons. Additional job creation, funding and training has already been discussed. I think in the longer term the answer must be more in the line of industrial development, which is outside the direct scope of my department, and meetings are taking place in Ottawa with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and my officials particularly to develop plans and to discuss further with the provincial authorities on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to draw attention once again to question 69 which was placed on the order paper nearly three calendar years ago, namely, on September 30, 1974. It is a simple question asking for straightforward facts, namely, how many trips the Prime Minister has taken at public expense since October 30, 1972, and, of that total, how many have been trips to political gatherings or for the purposes of private pleasure.

subtopic: POLICY STATEMENT ON RAIL PASSENGER SERVICES

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: POLICY STATEMENT ON RAIL PASSENGER SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, transportation for people is vitally important in Canada and we believe that Canadians themselves ought to be able to choose the method of travel which suits their own needs from among safe, sound systems. Since transportation is so important a matter for Canadians, we cannot waste our resources on unused, inefficient or duplicated systems.
We have operated extensive rail passenger services in Canada. However, they have been allowed to deteriorate so that Canadians no longer have a fair incentive to use them. This was in no way due to any fault on the part of those who operate the trains, but to a combination of management and government policies which could only produce losses and worsening service. It is my intention today to change that policy as far as the government is concerned and to outline an approach which will provide better service but in a narrower range of areas.
We are very conscious of the impact of these changes, both positive and negative, upon communities and upon the men and women who run our passenger trains. I have
Transportation
begun a process of consultation with their leaders. I plan to continue, and I hope, with the assistance of members of parliament, to consult with the workers and people to be directly affected, to ensure that we understand their views. Where adjustments are necessary, we plan to ensure that they are made with as much sense and sensitivity as possible. I expect, in particular, to develop plans to avoid hardship to workers affected by changes in service.
When the major elements of our transportation policy were announced in June of last year, we stated that Canadians must have an efficient transportation system providing a high degree of accessibility and equity of treatment for all users. Transportation must also support national and regional, social and economic objectives. The new transportation policy recognizes that areas exist where services are well developed and utilized. These services should be operated on a commercially viable basis and fares should be set through the efficient forces of competition and the marketplace. In other areas where services are required for social or developmental purposes but cannot achieve commercial viability, the government is prepared to provide leadership and assistance to develop the best possible level of efficiency.
We also emphasize throughout the new transportation policy that Canadians require the use of highway, rail, marine and air services to provide the best level of services at the lowest total cost, and that these modes of transportation must work together in the roles for which they are best suited. This policy has resulted from extensive consultations with the provinces, industry and labour. It recognizes regional differences and provides a framework in which positive action can be developed to move the commerce of the nation and provide for business and leisure travel.
As our research has progressed over the past year and we have considered the needs and costs of transportation, it has become clear that we cannot afford unnecessary duplication of facilities. This is particularly true at this time of financial restraint. We have also found that bus, air and rail, while they do compete, have distinct markets in which they have special advantages. It is our intention, as we further develop passenger policies, that each mode of transport be given the opportunity to develop these markets. This will provide Canadians with access to acceptable levels of service at the least total cost. Where a subsidy is required in support of regional and national goals, the most economically efficient mode will be used, and the impact of that subsidy on other modes of transport will be considered.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are not pleased with the railway passenger system as it currently exists. Losses amounted to $167 million in 1974 and they are increasing: they may amount to $400 million by 1980 if changes are not made. We are not alone in the world in this respect. Governments in almost every industrialized nation are wrestling with similar problems of mounting losses. Canada now has more miles of rail passenger services per capita than any other major nation. Many of our services meet high international standards in terms of amenities, speeds and fares. Revenues cover about one-third of the total costs of providing the services. Subsidies provided by the Canadian public

January 29, 1976
Transportation
are proportionately higher for passenger trains than they are for other forms of transportation.
The primary reason for this situation is that other forms of transportation, primarily the automobile, have proven more attractive to the public. The impression grew that passenger trains were obsolete and this in turn affected growth and the evolution and development of new equipment and techniques. We are left with a system designed for an earlier Canada.
Consider these examples, Mr. Speaker. About 20 per cent of the services operated carry 10 passengers or less on the average, 55 per cent less 47, or a bus load, and only 35 per cent more than 100. Over the year, only one-third of the seats offered are sold. At daily peak periods, about one-third of the fleet is actually in operation. There are over 2,000 miles of routes where CN and CP duplicate services, and duplicate terminals in many major cities. On transcontinental routes, more subsidy is currently being paid for fist-class services than for basic coach transportation.
One course of action recommended by some is the total elimination of rail passenger services and therefore the losses currently incurred. We believe, however, that rail service can fill a real need at a reasonable cost and that only if the service is desirable and efficient will we be able to test the real and future place for it among Canadians. We believe we can develop a better rail system, thereby avoiding some demands for highways and airports and the use of transportation systems that are less efficient in their use of energy and land.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that there are potentially three major roles for passenger trains, roles that can be filled at reasonable subsidy levels, provided services are improved and operated efficiently and economically. First are short to medium-distance services between major cities where rail offers the potential of trip times somewhere between those of automobiles, buses and aircraft; second are commuting trips in and about major cities for the movement of large numbers of people; and third are long distance trips across the breadth of the country where trains might provide a higher level of basic service than buses. Rail services should also be continued in those remote areas of our country where no reasonable transportation alternatives exist. These roles recognize the ability of trains to carry large numbers of people, to require minimum amounts of new land and, if well patronized and efficiently operated, to make good use of energy. Procedures are being established to determine the public's interest in improving these services.
However, Mr. Speaker, on some routes in Canada passenger trains do not serve the public well. In our view, bus and air transportation can often provide the public with better quality and more frequent services at lower cost. It is the government's intention to encourage the development of these services to replace passenger trains on routes where trains are poorly suited to the market or poorly patronized.
It is our intention to work toward an economically and socially justified national network of rail services. We propose that a basic network of intercity, transcontinental and commuter services, co-ordinated with air and bus
(Mr. Lang.]
service where possible, be implemented. This will provide Canadians with an opportunity to respond to improved services and for us to understand the nature and degree of this response.
Our work is also progressing on the project to upgrade service in the Windsor-Quebec corridor. This comparatively high volume market appears to have the potential for supporting a better service. Our understanding of the costs and markets has been significantly improved since the announcement of this project, and we have begun discussions with the provinces and the carriers on the potential improvements and the phasing of changes so that safety, speed, comfort, service and costs can all be developed to meet demand. We plan, if possible, to begin upgrading the service in the near future and, depending on negotiations, to announce shortly full details of a plan that will see new equipment operating at higher standards by 1979.
The rail passenger program we are proposing is an open consultative process which my statement today formally launches. We propose active consultations with the provincial governments in the planning of regionally-based passenger services, with labour representatives to ensure the best use of the valuable human resources involved, with industry, with the railroads, with other carriers and with the public at large. The government is asking the Canadian Transport Commission to hold hearings within the framework established by these policies and guidelines to determine public interests and concerns. To implement this phase of the program, Mr. Speaker, I will be tabling directives for the guidance of the Canadian Transport Commission. In parallel, Transport Canada will itself consult with carriers, labour, provinces and others concerning their areas of interest and concern. This work will form the basis for plans for the introduction of an improved basic network of rail services in Canada. As service improvements are implemented and subsidy per passenger decreased, the government is prepared to increase its subsidy from 80 per cent of losses to 100 per cent of losses provided that efficiency in management and operations can be demonstrated.
The purpose of this program, Mr. Speaker, is to create a transport system that supports economic and social goals on both national and regional levels. We will now expect Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and others to make management decisions to improve services. We also see these carriers making joint use of terminals and reservation systems, making schedules more sensitive to the regional markets, developing systems to change holiday and weekend demand so that most of the carriers' equipment is used on a continuing basis rather than on the few peak days per year, co-ordinating schedules between air, bus and rail to remove long stopovers, developing the demonstration project to evaluate advanced rail technology, furthering research in necessary roadbed improvements, and embarking on innovative passenger service marketing.
Through this approach we are giving the railways an opportunity to develop rail passenger services to serve markets willing to use and pay for the services. They will be asked to develop a system, with our assistance, that will better serve people who wish to use rail, and remove services that are unnecessary. Their challenge is to
January 29, 1976

improve service and operations by joint action where necessary, but under normal rail management. If the attractiveness and efficiency of service is not improved rapidly, we will have to consider another organization to provide rail passenger service in Canada.
In outlining this program, Mr. Speaker, we have presented a part of our passenger program. We announced last year that, starting in 1977, $100 million will be spent over five years in the purchase of rail commuter equipment. These two programs are integral parts of a series of initiatives that are being developed to assure that a total passenger policy meets our national and regional goals.
It is our intention to pursue improvements in the attractiveness, efficiency and economy of passenger trains in roles for which they are well suited and can be well patronized. In roles where passenger trains are poorly suited to the market or poorly patronized, our intention is to encourage other modes to replace them. In this manner we plan to improve transportation for Canadians and to control the deficits that are growing beyond acceptable levels. I emphasize that in doing this we seek the advice and the cooperation of the public, carriers, labour and the provinces.

That is also significant.
Perhaps we can draw some parallel with the airlines. I do not think many people in this country want to fly on 25-year-old aircraft which do not have proper scheduling. The parallel could be drawn in respect of passenger rail
Transportation

What is indicated is that ultimately, if we are going to travel on the railways, we will certainly be staying at railway hotels. Running through the document is a direct indication that the government has made up its mind to downgrade rail passenger services, and that downgrading appears to be a psychological expression of the kind of thinking at the present time in the Ministry of Transport.
As I said before, the minister's statement is significant in what it did not say, rather than what it said. I am not going to deal with all the election promises made, but the minister in charge of the Wheat Board probably campaigned with some of these same election promises. On June 18, 1974, in Cornwall, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that the Liberal government, if re-elected, would take over all national passenger services operated by Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway. The Prime Minister talked about forming a corporation and a piggyback service on our transcontinental line. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the government had no intention whatsoever of implementing these kinds of proposals. These were strictly political window-dressing to seduce voters at the time of the last election.
I know my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to mention the kind of thinking that takes place in the Ministry of Transport. We in this country are apparently to have airports coming out of our ears. We spent $1.45 billion on the airport at Mirabel. Although the Pickering airport was scrapped, or has been postponed, it was going to cost us another $400 million. The Malton terminal 2 building cost us $42 million in 1973 and a parking extension cost us $125 million. We have all this, yet the department is not putting any money into existing facilities in order to fix up rail passenger services in this country.
STOL is a perfect example of the kind of blind-headed philosophy the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the government have at the present time. It is running at a deficit, and would have been running at a much larger deficit were it not for the fact that civil servants have been instructed to use this facility between Ottawa and Montreal.
The minister mentioned the user pay concept this afternoon, and I suggest we will hear a lot more about this concept in the future. The minister, his deputies and officials in MOT should know that there is no form of transportation, no matter what it is, that operates on a strictly

user pay concept, and to single out railways and railway passenger service is a red herring. To do that in this case is totally unrealistic and I do not believe the Canadian public will swallow it.
It is interesting to note, when we talk about psychology, that maybe one of the reasons behind this rather blind-sided policy is the fact that in the past two or three years there have been over 40 studies carried out on all aspects of rail passenger service. In 1970 there was a CTC study of intercity passenger transportation which concluded that it was possible to upgrade the Montreal-Toronto rail route so as to provide a good, three-hour rail service between the two cities. In 1972 an MOT and railways study recommended the nationalization of all maritime rail passenger services. The study supposedly forecast annual savings of up to $8 million. In 1973 there was a study which indicated that through the use of LRC-type trains it would be possible to provide a one hour and fifteen minute service between Montreal and Ottawa, and that the service could possibly make a profit.
The studies continued until the last one, in October, 1975. At that time three new studies were started by MOT. One heading is, "What is equity service for bus, rail and air?" That study was by the MOT task force. Another study was headed, "Passenger transportation work program". That was conducted by MOT's passenger core group. Another was, "Possible improvements to rail passenger services in the corridor". That, too, was carried out by MOT's policy, planning and major projects group with the participation of CNR and CPR. The list goes on and on. The government continually has put its rail passenger transportation policies in some desk or on some shelf in the minister's office, in the deputy minister's office or somewhere in the Ministry of Transport.
In conclusion, I should like to say that in my opinion the government will regret the day it made this kind of a decision, for two reasons. First, there is the energy aspect and, second, there is the pollution aspect. Neither the minister nor anyone else can deny that the most efficient use of energy is for a reasonable, efficient and comfortable train system in this country. As we move into the latter part of the 1970s and the early 1980s, pollution will become more of a problem. I predict that within ten years we will come to the House of Commons and ask for a revitalized railway program something similar to the program which the Americans have at the present time. At that time, such a program will cost us hundreds of millions of dollars and we will have wasted much time, talent and energy.
I would hope the Canadian people would react somewhat violently to the proposals of the minister. In my opinion, the government has made the decision to cut down rail passenger service and will ask the CTC to ratify that decision through some kind of democratic process such as the minister described. This certainly will not be acceptable to this party.

Mr. Speaker, after many statements and announcements made over many months by this minister, his predecessor and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in and out of and during election campaigns, and since there has been a build-up of

expectation in the minds of the Canadian people that today we would hear an announcement of specific and solid policy whether we like it or not, that we would hear a decision had been made and specific action would be taken, we have today's statement. Instead of an announcement of specific and solid policy, we received from the same people who brought us the anti-inflation program- after they had given themselves a salary increase of $4,000 or $6,000-a transportation statement that does not meet the expectations I have mentioned. It repeats what we have heard dozens of times before. It is based on assumptions and conclusions that are false or, at best, misleading.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) mentioned- and I repeat it-that on June 7, 1974, the Prime Minister said that wage and price controls were too simplistic, too disastrous, in economic and social terms, to consider. On June 18, the Liberal party promised a revitalized intercity passenger rail service for Canada. They promised measures to encourage and facilitate Canadian design and production of quality intercity passenger service vehicles, systems, equipment and machinery. They promised a Canadian passenger transport corporation whose first priority would be to work on the introduction of high-speed passenger rail service in Canada. They even promised excursion trains across the country.
However, today the minister announces, in effect, the curtailment of rail passenger service. In spite of all the platitudes and phrases in that statement, in effect that is what he is announcing. What is at question no longer is the integrity of the minister, the Prime Minister or the government but, rather, their fitness to govern and their ability to cope with a modern economy with a modern transportation system.
The former minister described transportation in this country as a mess. He said that competition does not work. We are still in the same mess, and the same competition does not work. Today I am reminded of the stories-and they are accurate-that are told about old Bob Edwards when he ran the Calgary Eye-Opener. When Bob Edwards ran that newspaper he carried on a running battle with the CPR. Every time there was a CPR wreck, he put a photograph of the wreck on the front page of the paper.
When R. B. Bennett, who was legal counsel for the Canadian Pacific Railway, became leader of the Conservative party, Bob Edwards published a front page picture of R. B. Bennett in the Calgary Eye-Opener with the caption underneath "Another CPR wreck". Now, I would suggest to the media, they should publish a photograph of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on the front page of the newspapers across this country and call it "Another CPR wreck".
The minister, on the first page of his statement, made a major concession about what members of this House and members of the public have been saying for years: he said that the railways have been allowed to deteriorate so that Canadians no longer have a fair incentive to use them. That is true. Then he said:
This was in no way due to any default on the part of those who actually operate the trains but to a combination of management and government policies which could only produce losses and worsening service.
Transportation
Nowhere in this statement does the minister propose to correct those services. In no way does he propose to change the policies which he admits produced losses and worsening of service. Now that we have the confession on page one, the Minister of Transport goes on to say:
These services should be operated on a commercially viable basis, and fares should be set through the efficient forces of competition and the marketplace.
Mr. Speaker, that is what got us into this mess in the first place. One has only to look at a newpaper article in the Financial Post of January 17, where the minister is reported as saying: "That the user should pay is the key". If that is true, we not only kiss the railways goodbye but I ask the minister whether he is now saying that the users of Air Canada, CPR and the other airlines in this country will pick up the $600 million deficit, which will be the case for
1974-75, for the provision of air transportation services by the Government of Canada.
Is he also saying that the users of buses, which the government and the experts in the minister's department claim are paying their own way, will now be required to pay their own way? For example, there was a deficit last year of $1.2 billion, in terms of the revenue received and cost paid for the highway system in this country. So if the users are to pay, the minister has more bad news for many people.
Is the minister saying that the St. Lawrence Seaway deficit will be picked up by the users only? Is he saying that the tens of million of dollars in deficits in the operation of our harbours and ports will now be picked up entirely by the users? Mr. Speaker, if you think there was a mess before under the former minister of transport, can you visualize what is coming?
The minister's statement perpetuates the old problems. Successive governments, in preparing our transportation policy, have refused to take into account Canada's geography, its climate and the location of its people. This government continues to refuse to recognize these factors in transportation, which is an essential public service which everyone has to use. This service can no longer be operated under nineteenth century concepts of profitability, commercial viability and competition. That has gone out of style and out of existence; it is irrelevant and obsolete. Talk to the people of countries in Europe, talk to the Japanese, the Australians, and now even the Americans with their beginnings of a new railway transportation system: the are now admitting what European countries admitted 30 years ago, namely, that competition and profitability in the provision of an essential public service have no place in a decent society which needs transportation services to meet the needs of the population.
If what the minister says about competition, commercial viability and that only the user shall pay, is logical, then it would be equally logical to have two competing sewer systems and two competing water lines running under our streets; it would be logical to have two competing telephone systems and power lines. The principles of competition and commercial viability were thrown out of the window 100 years ago, but this economic transportation dinosaur still clutches onto this nineteenth century con-

The minister says that the subsidies provided by Canadian are proportionately higher for passenger trains than for other forms of transportation. That is a lie.

"Who do the people of Saskatoon think they are, that they should have a transcontinental rail service?"- that is what the minister and his experts think.
The minister's announcement means nothing more than the perpetuation of what we have had for decades. It means policies which will continue to discriminate against Canadians because of where they happen to live. I want to conclude by saying that since transportation is a public service and a public utility which everyone has to use, it should be-as is the case in dozens of countries of all political stripes-publicly owned, controlled and operated.

That service, under public control and ownership, should integrate all modes of transportation; but we submit that it must have as its first priority the provision of service, and it should provide maximum access to people all over the country as a matter of right, and not a privilege.
We consider that all other modes of transportation must be integrated with, and ancillary to, the essential ingredient in our transportation system, namely, the railways. Unless and until this or any other government of Canada does that, we will continue to have an inefficient transportation system. The announcement made by the minister today has provided no assurance that anything will be changed. To the contrary, it will increase the amount of terror in the minds and hearts of the people of Canada in terms of what is in store for them regarding the provision of transportation and what it will cost them.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the statement of the minister, but still with very much scepticism because if everything that has been said in the speeches made here these last ten years on the question of improving our transportation had materialized, Canada would have the best transport system in the world. I have a very good memory of the famous statements of the former Minister of Transport, who wanted to renovate everything and who in fact has not renovated anything at all. The best evidence is that he is now in charge of another department, namely environment. I hope that in his new department he would have people clean all the stations which have been boarded up as a result of mismanagement and which are falling apart while people talk about renovation.
Today the minister tells us: We are going to have regional studies. But who will be in charge? The minister says nothing about that. Will he still send groups of technocrats from big cities to study, for instance, the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region so that they can impose their conditions? Mr. Speaker, if such are the wishes of the minister, he should forget about these studies. If he really wishes to be serious, he should come and talk to the people of the area, and organize meetings and discussions on the best way to renovate our transport systems. The approach then would be realistic as it would mean talking with local people, residents and railway employees. I submit that this would be the first step in dealing with the service the minister recommends. But if on the other hand he still relies on a kind of ever burgeoning bureaucracy while maintenance staff decreases proportionally, then the minister is once more going to miss the boat-

-and there will not be any
serious change. Like all his other predecessors, he wants to suppress some lines of passenger trains. Passengers are always victimized, as if they were not part of the railway service, so entitled to get services as taxpayers. We have nothing against freight service. Freight is a very profitable activity in our area. But for 15 years now we have been told that our passenger service was going to end and our people are very upset by this eventuality.


It is my opinion that with serious surveys, it is possible to prove that a passenger service, not the one that we have now, which is completely obsolete, but a really efficient one will attract a great deal of customers, because I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that I have been travelling by train for these last 15 years.
We hear people who after their second or third trip by train say on their arrival: "They had me once, but never ever again." Well, this means that service or safety is deficient. We noted again this winter a lack of safety and I will return to the matter later. The minister has stated once more that he will close some lines. Perhaps some of them ought to be cancelled. However, in areas where it is the only reliable means of transport available, closing those lines should be out of question. The withdrawal of sleeping cars has also been mentioned. The minister is trying to justify himself because for years now I found that the railway company was merely interested in its hotel system. It would then be easier to fill those hotels set up throughout Canada and worth umpteen million dollars. It is likely that they were beginning to empty, so trains would stop there and passengers would have to stay overnight in hotels and be fed. He may be right on this account if he wants to save these hotels.
Now, we are wondering about offices. I live in the Sague-nay-Lac-Saint-Jean area. A few years ago, you may recall that the servocentre campaign was launched. One was created in Jonquiere and another in Saint-Felicien. Now, they want to close the latter and maintain the former, which was built, it has to be said, at the cost of millions of dollars, while I always stressed that Jonquiere was not the proper site for a servocentre. The central junction should have been Chibougamau, the Dolbeau junction. The Jonquiere junction was at Chambord. But the officials in Montreal have never been able to understand that. Never. Today, they realize, after spending a great deal of money that the Saint-Felicien servocentre is not longer any good. After three, four or five years, it is no longer any good. They are looking towards Jonquiere to build some extensions. After having bought warehouses which are no longer used, they have to rent them to the City of Jonquiere to get rid of them, and it is impossible to come back to the central point. I call the minister's attention to this problem so that when he will commission studies in our area his research workers will geographically locate the central point of the area. They will find that will reduce expenses first of all and then improve the services. The railway will then be able to tell the population that they provide good services, and not services like the ones we have had those last few years and again this winter.
This winter, Mr. Speaker, passengers from Chambord have travelled aboard a non heated train at temperatures of 40 below zero. The train had to go to Montreal without any heat because there is no more service in Chambord. Previously there was some storage, repairs could be done, there was a garage, but there is nothing of that today. They have to go to Montreal to have a pump repaired. So all passengers had to wrap themselves up in blankets on their way to Montreal. That happened three or four times, that I know of. It happens again and again, and nobody wants to correct it. Engines stay outdoors during winter because
Transportation
there is no garage. There are garages, yes, three beautiful garages, but they are closed. They are not heated. Engines are covered with ice. Then they start for Montreal. They use hammers to break the ice. They they start for Montreal. One engineer told me recently: To go up to Chibougamau, we use five engines, and we come back with one or two, because the others are all broken. There are no maintenance men left. The service no longer works. These things must be known, but nobody talks about them. How can you expect improvements?
Moreover, those who might speak up cannot do so because they stand to lose their jobs; and so it goes. Does anyone believe the people who took the train this winter will do so again next winter? Never, no, never! Yet, that run could so easily be improved. Unfortunately, it takes 12, 18 and even 20 hours to get to Montreal when, with a normal train, it could easily be done in six. I would even say, very easily; every engineer says so.
So, what is the problem? At every turn, you see a little inspector of 24 or 25, fresh out of school, coming to impose new rules upon old employees who know ten times as much as he does. To my mind, someone will have to start using his brains and put an end to the game of the small bureaucrat. The government will have to come out of its lethargy, quit putting its trust in those people and try to appoint people who are serious enough to be capable of giving the services needed by the people.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, because I would not like to be too long, all we want is good service. One would believe that government officials, especially those of the railway company, have forgotten above all that the railroad is paid by taxpayers and that in return they have to provide the necessary services to the population. This is all forgotten. In my opinion, the word "service" has been forgotten. It is far away from their minds.
When you think of services, you have to think of prices. To rent a regular small bed, it now costs $17. I cannot see a journeyman going to Montreal who can afford the luxury of a bed which costs $34 return, apart from his ticket. Prices must therefore be in line with services. Finally, safety must be provided. The passenger must feel safe. There should not be any events, like those we experienced last winter. However, I talked about it before the House, but nothin was changed. We have the oldest cars of the area, and they blame people for not taking the train.
But I can very well understand why a person who has taken the train once won't do it again.
Therefore I ask the minister to have his officials examine this matter, in order to provide people with modern travelling carriages and later to appoint responsible people, local people, to advise him. Local officials will be able to help him if he wishes to do a good job. On the other hand if he only wishes to follow the path of the former ministers who have preceded him, we must expect the same disappointments we are experiencing now.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for having the courage to ouline his policy for us and we are awaiting the results.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the House adjourned yesterday I had remarked that, should the government's clairvoyance regarding Bill C-68 fail to justify itself, Canadians would be faced with one of two alternatives-reduced health care services or increased taxes. In other words, if medical costs increase at a higher rate than that contemplated by the 1975-76 budgetary ceilings, the provinces will be forced to seek the very solutions which the federal government deemed undesirable in 1969.
There is no question that the unilateral action of the federal government has outraged the provinces. Their immediate reaction was to care for a cessation of consultation in connection with all cost-sharing programs of the federal government. If the government's ploy in introducing this legislation was to bring the provinces back to the bargaining table, as has been suggested, it is now clear that this ploy was completely misdirected.
Accompanying the unilateral approach to decision-making is the entire issue of arbitrariness. If Bill C-68 is passed, the ceilings established in the bill will become statutory. While one of the primary principles of responsible government is that parliament cannot bind its successor, political realists realize that reversal of decisions previously made is usually a long and difficult task. What will happen if the ceilings on spending are too low? What if the desired standards for health care simply cannot be maintained, given the bill's restrictions? It appears the figures have been pulled out of a hat; no explanation or investigation accompanied these figures. In short, the ceilings can be criticized because there is no indication that the percentage delimiters are appropriate and also because there is no room for flexibility. The government has made open-ended provision for ceilings and, should they be incorrect, there is little room for compensation.
Last year, national medical care expenditures ran at $1.37 billion. Expenditures for this year cannot yet be

realized, but obviously three possibilities exist: outlay could increase marginally, or as projected, or quite markedly. Since what happens financially in this year will dictate federal contributions for the years to come, one again can only speculate what could happen even if the provinces' budgetary outlay stayed inside the guidelines.
The government has made the argument that the imposition of ceilings on the federal contribution to medicare will not cause undue strain on provincial coffers, will not result in reduced health care services, and that the guidelines could encourage provincial restraint and provide a positive input into planned budgetary forecasting. This could only occur if the price of physicians' services likewise did not rise above the budgetary ceilings. In turn, if physicians' services do not rise above the ceilings, then the government has, in fact, imposed an effective wage control on a single, identifiable professional group. It is not difficult to see the blatant, discriminatory nature of such a move.
Another point which can be raised deals with doctors' salaries and taxes. The government has decried the increased costs of health care. We have seen that in the medical care field this documentation is basically without foundation. However, even if one was to concede that medical expenses should be curbed, it must be remembered that the federal government receives a substantial return on its capital outlay for medicare in the form of physicians' taxes.
In 1972, the average taxable income of physicians in Canada was $41,105. By inflating this figure by the increase in medical expenses we could speculate that doctors are earning approximately $50,000 per annum. From the last figures available in 1973, there were 36,095 physicians in Canada. National gross physicians' incomes can therefore be estimated at roughly $1.17 billion. Given the present tax structure, each doctor in Canada would pay approximately $9,600 in federal taxes, equalling $346.5 million in total tax payment to the federal treasury, or 51 per cent of the total federal payments to the provinces for medical care in 1974. In this light, the government's complaint of budgetary strain due to costs of medicare becomes increasingly hollow.
There is no question that the reasons for imposing ceilings on medical costs are fairly flimsy. It is not possible to forecast accurately what is going to happen to medical care in Canada in view of the changes suggested in Bill C-68. This point has been mentioned before and should be emphasized again. Since the long-term condition of health services in Canada is dependent on so many countervailing variables and non-quantifiable exigencies, it is increasingly difficult to predict the future of this field without blind confidence. However, this is exactly what the government has done in introducing Bill C-68.
In conclusion, the government has given itself a narrow and restrictive course to follow in the years ahead. It certainly cannot claim to be prophetic, yet the minister and his colleagues have committed themselves to an empirical approach to health care financing, thereby severely limiting their ability to deal with problems in the unforeseen or unforeseeable future.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join this debate today on the medicare budget,

Bill C-68, not only as a physician and pharmacist but also as a fellow citizen concerned with the effectiveness and efficiencies of national spending. I think it is important to start by looking at our medical care system. First, the previous system. Until recent years Canada shared with the world a traditional system of health care even then one of the best. People lived a simpler life and only when definitely ill and unable to carry on went for help to a health professional, usually a physician or medical doctor. Hospital remained a last resort.
As with any system, there were advantages and disadvantages. They paid the doctor directly on a professional fee for service basis, similarly the hospital. There developed a proud system of responsibility and mutual respect. Eventually private insurance schemes became available but the same basic sense of values continued. Administration was still simple and privately financed. Undoubtedly, some inequities did exist, inequities between rich and poor, between those with serious illness and those fortunate enough to remain healthy. Some people probably hesitated to seek care when they needed it.
However, in my own experience, people were looked after as well as possible, within the limitations of the time, the state of the art and science. Generally, no one in need was turned away and unpaid debts were absorbed by doctors and hospitals. The so-called Robin Hood system was accepted-take more from the rich to cover the poor. Medicine was not only a respected profession but "the noble profession". Ironically, medicine in the old days seemed to enjoy more respect while having less capability to help the ill. However, with changing social values in recent years, even with increasing general affluence and more ability to pay, such a traditional system came under increasing criticism and increasing public aversion to anything resembling charity.
Next, the present system. The concept of comprehensive prepaid plans grew stronger, beyond the limits of private plans, and public pressure led to more and more government involvement. In spite of concerns in both the public and private sector, we seemed to become more and more involved in open-ended plans as well. Undoubtedly these were politically popular during the existing affluent times when they started. As well, they probably represented an easier type of plan to administer.
Deterrent fees have been considered and even tried. I personally find many people, including doctors, feel they are still worth a try. However, many others feel that not only do they not work but they are unjust, with the wrong people deterred from seeking help-the needy, the old, the poor, the submissive. Our open-ended plan was founded on the honour system, on values presumed to exist, unlikely to lead to overuse or misuse. Now, with mounting costs, we wonder if our trust was misplaced.
People have not been trained to restrain their use of the system. In fact, they have been encouraged in recent years to increase their use of it in the name of good, modern, scientific medicine, especially preventive aspects such as regular physical examinations and cancer tests. We probably have been sensitive to mutual criticism at the thought of suggesting less use of health services, including both sides in the doctor-patient relationship. In an expanding
January 29, 1976

economy, an affluent society with constantly rising expectations is not likely to accept limits on services gladly.
However, times have changed, the economy has slowed and pressure has developed against government size and spending. In June, 1975, the Minister of Finance introduced certain major spending restraints, the first seen in many years and the first of many to come, probably. In the medical field it involved two areas: hospital care, including diagnostic services, and medicare, which includes mainly doctors' services in both the office and on house calls, plus administrative expenses for both.
Over the next three years increases in the federal contribution to medicare were to be scaled down annually to 14 per cent, 12.5 per cent and 10 per cent calculated to cover a decreasing inflation rate and a 1.5 per cent rate of population increase. It was not stated how this would affect doctors' fees and total incomes, a matter of subsequent concern to doctors and, surprisingly, also to provincial governments which had also been expressing alarm over growing health and welfare budgets.
Until the anti-inflation program came along doctors were also concerned that they would be the only Canadians under income restraints and therefore the victims of discrimination. Now they are concerned, like everyone else, about income guidelines, but also whether the discrimination will remain after the anti-inflation program ceases.
Still, how would a medicare bill like C-68 relate to a general restraint bill like C-73 in the meantime? The medical profession also points out that theirs is one of the few professions with a publicly-standardized fee schedule more readily subject to controls. Ontario doctors, for example, have been held and have agreed to an average 5 per cent increase in their fees over the last five years, including increased costs of practice, while inflation has been increasing at 10 per cent. An annual 10 per cent increase in fees over the next three years over and above the percentage increase in costs of medical practice according to the guidelines might then be seen as acceptable as long as this limit were applied consistently to other Canadians, and as long as increased costs were exempted as is to be the case for other businesses.
However, doctors incomes also depend on how many patients they see in a year, as well as their level of individual fees. Should a limit be put on their total income and, either way, how does one distinguish between true productivity, which is to be encouraged, as against unnecessary, expensive overservicing, which is to be discouraged? Personally, I believe only the profession itself is capable of making the distinction, and even then only with great difficulty.
Many factors can legitimately and sometimes temporarily increase the annual volume of a doctor's practice beyond his control: the natural growth of his practice, especially for a doctor just getting established, or one changing location, loss of a partner, or an increase of illness in the community-and he should not be penalized for this. If he is, his patients and the community can also suffer. Fair treatment is also more conducive to a valuable profession such as a doctor managing an expensive social system well.

A surtax on total income might cut costs and might even discourage misuse of the health system, but is the price worth it in terms of lost productivity and a demoralized profession? By the way, it is also important that income equitability exist with the medical profession, that is, between geographical areas like provinces and between specialists and GPs.
Let me say a word about health care spending. The fast-growing Canadian health and welfare bill is now taking about one-third of all government spending. The federal budget for this department will be around $10 billion, and the Ontario budget around $3 billion for 1976, in proportion to population. At present, the federal government is committed to pay half the cost of whatever hospital and medical expenses the provinces incur.
At three federal-provincial conferences between 1971 and 1973, Ottawa offered the provinces a formula under which they would receive a per capita lump sum every year tied to increases in the gross national product rather than to increases in health costs, but the provinces rejected it each time, convinced that they would lose if they accepted it.
The federal Minister of National Health and Welfare Minister (Mr. Lalonde) has announced, in principle, extending federal support to some lower cost health services beyond those covered at present, but which ones have not yet been announced. The changes are expected to slow the rate of increase in health costs. These other services, presumably less expensive, are to conform to existing legislation,-the Medical Care Act, and the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Alternatives to acute hospital care, such as nursing homes, home care and ambulatory services will be considered, but provinces will first be expected to give a firm commitment on their plans in the hospital and medical fields over the next few years.
Support for dental and drug care programs is not considered possible at this time, and because of the magnitude of any such programs they would have to be considered separately as the economy improves. Such an agreement should meet the demands of most provincial governments which have been complaining about the present health plan as too rigid financially, which prevents funds from being used efficiently. In addition, cost-saving efforts must go beyond medical bills and place more emphasis on prevention, on environment and behavioural risks such as automobile accidents, physical neglect and occupational risks as outlined in the ministry's "New Perspectives on Health for Canadians".
However, on the professional scene, hospital costs are increasing faster than medical costs, that is, those in the doctor's office or on house calls. Ontario health minister Frank Miller complains that hundreds of hospital beds are now empty, but hospital boards and doctors are not keen to use them for older chronic patients, perhaps due to longstanding patterns of practice. Average hospital budgets in Ontario were up 15 per cent for 1975, nearly twice the rate allowed under provincial ceilings. In return, Mr. Miller is threatening to close some hospitals and decrease the power of hospital boards. An average hospital bed costs up to $20,000 per year to operate but, ironically, closing a ward saves only $8,500 per bed per year.

On the other hand, the Canadian Medical Association claimed that doctors needed a 14 per cent increase to boost their salaries by 10 per cent in 1975. Dr. Bette Stephenson, former president of the Canadian Medical Association and now an Ontario politician, said that this would still only give doctors two-thirds of the predicted income increase for the average Canadian. Under OHIP, Ontario doctors were granted only a 7.75 per cent increase in 1974 and a 4 per cent increase in 1975. She said that although government figures show Canada's doctors are the highest paid profession, at $68,000 in annual payments, costs of practice ranging from 40 per cent to 75 per cent, and income tax near 50 per cent, reduce that amount to a disposable income of $26,000. Costs of practice, as well as nursing and hospital staff salaries, have increased sharply in the meantime.
Regardless of these figures, the profession of medicine- in spite of reports emerging from Ontario-seems willing to conform with the anti-inflation program as long as other Canadians do also. They have difficulty understanding the new medicare bill on budget restraints, partly because they are not clear how it affects doctors' incomes and other items of expenditure, and partly because they are not clear how it is affected by the anti-inflation guidelines for doctors' incomes.
Canadian Medical Association officials seem most reasonable in their negotiations and admit to a satisfactory working relationship with the Minister of National Health and Welfare. They acquitted themselves well in recent parliamentary committee meetings. Co-operation and optimism are certainly the order of the day in this relationship. The Toronto Globe and Mail, in its lead editorial on January 16, 1975, made the following comments under the title "Philosophies of Health":
Costs and political philosophies. These are the basis of the conflicts which divide provinces and provinces, as well as provinces and the federal government, on matters concerning health services for Canadians.
Medicare as it was established by Ottawa has proved enormously costly, without being flexible enough to provide some services that are needed or to put the accent on prevention rather than care.
Mr. Lalonde has agreed in principle to extend federal support to some other services, and a committee will work on the problem in the next several months.
It will be an advance if more health can be preserved or recovered at less cost. The cost of medical and hospital care, under the present formula, is increasing so rapidly that it is jeopardizing provincial budgets.
At no time, but particularly in a time of inflation, should Canada be advancing upon costly, universal, open-ended plans. What public money there is should be devoted to meeting the needs of those who cannot provide for themselves.
The other difficulty with universal plans for a country as disparate as Canada is that they are too inflexible to meet regional ones.

The editorial also points out differences of opinions between the provinces. Wealthy ones like Ontario and Quebec want only a larger share of personal income tax revenues. In contrast, the maritimes, Saskatchewan and British Columbia want more universal, shared-cost programs, for example, prescription drugs and dental care. Shared plans are seen adversely by some as interfering with the local setting of priorities; by others, beneficially as providing badly needed funds. In other words, some can afford to be independent and some cannot. Each approaches the same problem from his own vested interests. Fair enough, but it does not square exactly with national unity. Furthermore, it says a province like Alberta, currently flush with money, may not mind expensive programs like modern hospitals thrust on them by Ottawa while, ironically, the formerly reigning province of Ontario is now feeling the pinch and might prefer the cheaper chronic beds or home care programs. In light of these complexities, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have apparently promised not to impose any more universal programs on the provinces; hopefully, not even on the country.
The government has already run into trouble by suggesting what it believes is a generally reasonable, over-all limit on the rate of increase of medicare and has served statutory notice of a desire to renegotiate the hospital plan. The Globe and Mail editorial, even with the wisdom of hindsight, raises more questions than answers. In its retrograde, conservative way it suggests the return of a different plan for every province, a welfare-type plan for the needy, which is usually regarded these days as cold charity, and the accompanying expensive and fragmented system of private plans for all others. As Eliza Doolittle would say: "Not bloody likely".
Now I should like to say a word on the immigration of foreign doctors. Another aspect raised has been restrictions on the immigration of doctors to Canada, but not only for reasons of saving money; there are other concerns. One reason is to try to supply doctors to rural and remote areas of the country where they are in short supply. Another pressure is to permit more places in the medical schools for the children of existing Canadians. The immigration aspects are federal, the others provincial, but apparently the move has the support of all federal and provincial ministers involved.
The Ontario health minister proposed the action based on a full brief which he presented at the January, 1975, federal-provincial health ministers' conference in Ottawa. In 1973, 1,170 doctors immigrated to Canada, almost as many as the 1,326 who graduated from Canadian medical schools, while many well qualified Canadian students were turned away. Most foreign doctors, like immigrants in general, come to Ontario; but Ontario, at a ratio of one doctor per 585 people, is already well staffed compared to the World Health Organization recommendation of one per 650. The recent increase in doctors in Canada seems to be related to the introduction of medicare.
It is proposed that foreign doctors be treated like other immigrants, that they be barred unless they have a job waiting for them here or unless they commit themselves to part of the country where they are needed. Mr. Miller proposed that the flow to Ontario needs to be stemmed.
January 29, 1976

Each province should be able to declare whether it needs certain types of doctors, or any doctors at all, with federal immigration officials acting accordingly. Only Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and the Northwest Territories have recently been below recommended levels of doctors. A profession like medicine is otherwise self-regulating. Regulations have recently been tightened so that other immigrants would be needed regardless of educational qualifications. Only doctors and university teachers were exempted. No new legislation will be required for further tightening.
Now may I say a word about the doctor's actual situation. Canadian doctors claim that increases in medical fee schedules in recent years have not kept up to other factors such as the rate of inflation, other peoples' salary increases and the costs of new, expensive medical procedures. They also feel that official statistics and press reports have overstated their true average take-home pay by eliminating incomes under $30,000 per year, whereas many fulltime, regular practitioners actually do make less than $30,000. The proportion of Canada's GNP spent on medical services in Canada has apparently declined from 1.3 per cent in 1971-72 to 1.1 per cent in the 1975-76 forecasts. However, the hospital insurance contribution has increased at an annual rate of 18 per cent during the comparable four-year period, partly due to higher wage awards for hospital staff.
Health care costs have also been increased by increased utilization or patient demand for services, some of which may well be unnecessary and represent a potential area for cost reductions. Canada, after all, is one of the healthiest countries in the world. Doctors are busy enough, without doing unnecessary work. When they receive adequate fees they can take better care of both their patients and themselves. The health care system then works better and neither the doctors nor health budgets become exhausted.
I have some more figures on the situation of doctors, but in view of the time I shall leave it at this for the present. The government has proposed a number of amendments. The first is that the exact ceilings are to be set for two years only. Second, there will be provision for increases for new, important classes of services. Third, there will be a three-year exemption from the ceiling for new insured services. I think these are all very worth-while amendments which deserve the support of all of us.
It being six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude my remarks at this point.
