speakeroldname: Mr. Robert C. Coates (Cumberland-Colchester North) moved
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
that Bill C-265, to amend the Canada Pension Plan, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is quite a while since I first introduced this bill in the House. At the time I introduced it, I introduced a companion bill relating to the right of participants who had applied for disability pensions under the Canada Pension Plan to secure assistance of a legal nature in presenting their case, in view of the fact that the government was appearing before the commissions that were set up, represented by legal officers from the federal government. The minister agreed to the concept contained in the bill relating to legal assistance for applicants, and I was therefore able to withdraw that bill which was incorporated in government legislation.
This particular bill relates to the fact that the minister has available to him certain powers to appeal decisions that have been handed down by boards established under the legislation, and it was then my opinion, and it continues to be so, that the minister should not have this right, in view of the fact that the legislation calls for the establishment of certain committees under government legislation and that their decisions should be firm and final when they find in favour of an applicant.
Section 85(1) of the Canada Pension Plan provides:
An applicant or beneficiary or the minister, if dissatisfied by a decision of a review committee under section 84, may with the leave of the chairman of the Pension Appeals Board, appeal from the decision of a review committee to the Pension Appeals Board within 90 days from the day the decision is communicated to him or within such longer period as the Pension Appeals Board upon application made to it within those 90 days may allow.
The objective of this bill is to eliminate that portion of the section which reads "or the minister". In other words, the minister from this moment on, if the bill is adopted by the House, would no longer have the right to appeal. I think it would be appropriate to explain to the House the basis on which I initiated this bill, because it is very significant so far as I am concerned; it is as significant today as it was at the time I first introduced the bill.
Short of war, there is nothing more dehumanizing than big government in action. It is everywhere. It reveals itself in many forms. Businessmen call it red tape. Statistics Canada has been its chief instrument in the production of red tape. So long as it sticks to forms and statistics and commits the nation to computers, it is hard to fight, for all these acts are in the name of efficiency. Efficiency is constantly stressed in government circles but, unfortunately, is never produced. The system has become very sophisticated with its gadgetry, but is as inefficient today as it was in the horse and buggy days, and one only needs to refer to the new, computerized unemployment insurance scheme to know what I mean.

But what outrages me and many others in this nation is that when an ordinary citizen becomes a victim of big government, that citizen and the members of his family are deprived of those things they have a right to receive. It becomes even more disgusting when it is discovered that big government has used a member of parliament, who happens to also be a minister of the Crown, as the instrument to achieve its objective.
Deverne MacDonald is a young man, 37 years of age, married, with three children. He resides in the small community of Westchester, Cumberland county, Nova Scotia. He was an employee of the CNR as a sectionman until uncontrollable diabetes forced him out of the labour force. The days ahead are bound to be very difficult for Deverne MacDonald and his family. Our social justice system is still not geared for such situations. The best evidence of this fact is that Mr. MacDonald and his family are trying to survive on $200 per month. That breaks down to $40 per month per individual.
Mr. MacDonald, when informed of the extent of his disability, applied for a Canada Pension Plan disability pension. His application was rejected. That fact does not surprise me. In order to qualify for this particular pension you must have one foot in the grave and the other on a banana peel. Mr. MacDonald applied for this pension in January, 1971, and was informed of the rejection of his application in December, 1971. Mr. MacDonald appealed that decision. It was heard by what is known as the review committee. In May, 1972, this committee found in Mr. MacDonald's favour. After 18 months it appeared that he would secure some additional assistance. But that was not to be his fate. No less a personage than the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), then minister of national health and welfare, appealed the decision of the review committee to another body, the Pension Appeals Board.
The review committee is composed of three persons, one appointed by the minister, the second by the applicant-in this case, Mr. MacDonald-and the third by the two appointed members. The third person acts as chairman. But their decision did not satisfy the minister. He may say he took this action on behalf of his department. But the minister, not his department, took the action, and if he had so deemed it, the action would not have been taken.
On investigation I learned that the favourable decision of May, 1972, would either be confirmed or rejected in either April or June, 1973. That means 2Vi years after the man who was disabled first made application for a disability pension. It will probably be years from the time Mr. MacDonald made application for a disability pension, because he needed it then, to the date when a decision will be rendered on the minister's appeal. Who will render the decision? The Pension Appeals Board is composed of four judges who render a service through this board when they are not involved in their own court responsibilities. The judges are located in different parts of the country: one is from British Columbia, the second from the prairies, and two are from the province of Quebec. The board requires the attendance of three of the four judges. The board also has a registrar. The judges and the registrar will probably hold the hearing in Truro, Nova Scotia.

Along with the board will come a battery of lawyers and doctors, probably from Ottawa. Just imagine the expense involved in making a determination, initiated by the minister, as to whether an individual who is disabled as far as his doctors are concerned is disabled in the minds of a group of bureaucrats and judges pulled across Canada into Nova Scotia to make a decision whether to allow this particular individual to have a pension or not to have a pension. Mr. MacDonald, a man who has tried to live and to maintain his family on $200 per month has to leave Westchester, go to Truro, walk into a courtroom and face this battery of lawyers, doctors and judges because a minister in this House determined that he should not have something which an appointee on a board, whom the minister appointed, said he should. That is the situation.
What happened? The objective of the minister was to take away the right of this particular individual to have a pension to which the review committee said he was entitled. That is a pretty sad situation, and it is happening over and over again. I remember at the time this case came up, Donald Maclnnis, who at that time was a member of parliament, informed me that there were two similar situations in his constituency. During the 1972 election campaign he had to take time out to go before that hearing because the two individuals in his constituency could not afford lawyers and had to go there by themselves to be cross-examined by federal government-paid lawyers and before the group of judges who had been paid to go there. No doubt they were getting a mighty good fee on top of that for sitting. What happened in both those cases? One of them was a man who had three heart attacks, and his appeal was thrown out. In other words, he was disqualified from receiving the pension which an earlier committee had determined he should receive.
The fate of Mr. MacDonald was not any better than the fate of the individual in Mr. Maclnnis's constituency, because in the case of Mr. MacDonald it was said that even if he did have uncontrollable diabetes, according to their decision he could not qualify for a pension under the disability section of the Canada Pension Plan. It is difficult enough for an individual in this country to maintain himself and keep himself employed when he is healthy, but when he is faced with a situation where he has a disability which is so severe that he cannot work, and a minister of the Crown overrules a board which the minister himself set up, which said he should have a pension, it is a pretty sad commentary on life in this nation today, and certainly on the government. That is why I call it big government, government which does not think, worry or care about the people in this nation.
I think it is in the best interests of this parliament and in the best interests of the minister to eliminate his right to appeal a decision of the review committee in those cases where a favourable decision is rendered by the review committee.
As a matter of fact, it is my belief that the bureaucrats in the department are using the minister's name in order to try to do something which the minister, if he knew the full facts of the matter, would not do in the first place. We would be doing the minister, and certainly every individual who contributes to the Canada Pension Plan, a favour if
Canada Pension Plan
we eliminated this very iniquitous section of the act. Therefore, I hope hon. members will assist me in having this bill referred to committee, so that all members of parliament can examine it and determine if it is in the best interests of Canadians, generally speaking, to eliminate the minister's right in this particular way.
Big government is something we like to ignore. Sometimes we can. Deverne MacDonald and his family could not, and should not have had to face the fact of life they faced then and face today, unfortunately, because of a decision of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde).

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very technical point which is being proposed in Bill C-265 put forward by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), and just before getting into the details I should like to make one observation. In his comments about big government, I think the hon. member was indicating some of the derogatory points about big government, and I am sure we can all agree that, like anything which gets rather big, there are disadvantages built into the system. However, I think one of the advantages, or one of the interesting things to see, is that an item like this can come before the nation, and can be brought in great detail, about the individual circumstances of one particular person, Mr. Deverne MacDonald. I think it is a strong point for our system that Mr. MacDonald's problems can come before the parliament of this nation in this way. Although we have big government, there are still, hopefully, opportunities for matters of this kind to be discussed in this forum.
Bill C-265 proposes the deletion of the minister's prerogative to appeal a decision or a recommendation made by a tribunal. This is a fairly serious thing, and we must consider it very carefully because it is important that decisions on matters of this kind, made by tribunals of this sort which are only set up for the particular circumstances involved, do not create precedents which could have implications and serious consequences to many more people across the country. As the hon. member mentioned, the amendment is identical to that contained in an earlier bill sponsored by him and put before this House in 1973.
To put the implications in perspective, I think we must recall the origins and the historical development of the Canada Pension Plan, another creature of big government but, I think, a creature we are all rather happy to have. This is important in order for us to appreciate the complexities of the program itself. The Canada Pension Plan came into being in 1965. The enactment of the program was the culmination of a long series of legislation aimed at providing alternative forms of income security for old people in Canada. In fact, the subject of income assistance for the elderly had been a topic of parliamentary debate since the early days of this century, and silent witness to those debates can be found in the statutes.
It was recognized that in our complex society many aspects of everyday life can place an individual and his or her family in financial difficulties: for example, imperfect knowledge of labour markets, lack of education and adequate training, poor judgment, poor health, extraordinary

January 29, 1976
Canada Pension Plan
events, and one could go on and on. In consequence, it was found that despite the enactment of the rather innovative old age security pension plan, a large proportion of Canada's old people were still having to rely on public assistance. As a result, a three-pronged approach to income security for the elderly was put into place. These included an enrichment of the universal old age security pension and a gradual lowering of the eligibility age for this particular pension to 65.
There was also the introduction of the comprehensive social insurance plan for retirement, disability and survivors, called the Canada Pension Plan, and the enactment of the guaranteed income supplement for the aged to provide minimum income support for those unable to participate in the plan and those retiring before benefits available under the Canada Pension Plan matured. In some provinces, including my own, there has been an additional supplement. In Ontario this is referred to as "the Gains" plan, which adds to those benefits provided federally so that there is a minimum income assured to all residents of the province when they reach the age of retirement.
An examination of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, 1964-65, and the white paper on the Canada Pension Plan, 1964, reveals the following information about the intended general trusts of the plan: to provide a contributory pension program for Canadian workers with as comprehensive coverage as practicable; to provide basic pensions that would still leave room for private pensions and for personal initiative; to provide reasonable minimum levels of income to retired persons at normal retirement ages, to persons who become disabled and to the survivors of people who die; to provide earnings-related benefits; to provide flat rate benefits in addition to earnings-related benefits to the disabled and to the survivors of contributors for whom flat rate old age security benefits were not available, so as to assist the lower income groups, and to ensure provision of pensions that are related to general earnings levels at the time of retirement and to the levels of prices during retirement.
Thus, the Canada Pension Plan was expected to provide a central means by which contributions would be collected from employers, employees and the self-employed so that the working population could insure themselves and their families against three of the most common contingencies resulting in long-term financial hardships, namely, death, disability and retirement. The foregoing clearly demonstrates the breadth and complexity of this legislation and one can speculate upon the administrative difficulties experienced in applying this ambitious program.
To ensure fair and equitable treatment for all applicants and beneficiaries alike within the complex legislative framework, the Canada Pension Plan provides for a three-level appeal system. This was referred to in part by the honourable member. I should just like to enunciate it again. First, an applicant or beneficiary who is dissatisfied with the initial decision as to entitlement or the amount of that entitlement may appeal to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) for reconsideration of that decision. That is the first level of appeal.

Second, should the minister decide to maintain the original decision, then the applicant or beneficiary may appeal the ministerial decision to a review committee. A review committee is a locally constituted body of three people, one chosen by the appellant, one by the minister, and the third, the chairman, selected by the other two members.
Third, if either party to a review committee appeal, that is to say, the minister or the applicant or beneficiary, is dissatisfied with a committee decision, then either may, with leave, appeal that decision to the Pension Appeals Board. I think this is the point in question, whether the employee should still have that privilege or not. The Pension Appeals Board is the final stage of the appeal process.
It is clear that there must be a level of appeal for the minister beyond the review committee stage, since that person is charged with the responsibility of applying the terms of the Canada Pension Plan in a fair and consistent manner to the more than seven million contributors subject to the plan. I think we must bear in mind at all times the figure of seven million people involved. This is because the implementation of a review committee decision- which committee is most often a group of lay people and has no judicial authority beyond that stated in the Canada Pension Plan-in a particular case could mean, in effect, that the law would be applied to an individual in a way different from the application of that law in all other similar circumstances.
That is the point I was referring to at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, the importance of ensuring that a decision is not made by the appeal group that would then act as a precedent which would affect many other cases across the country. In these instances, a decision must then be taken whether the application is to be as the review committee believes it to be, or as the minister has been advised. Accordingly, the act provides for the Pension Appeals Board to act as a forum for the reaching of such a decision. At that level they can look at the situation and consider it in terms of its national implications.
Because of this function and because of the binding nature of its decisions, the Pension Appeals Board is made up of a chairman and vice-chairman who are judges of either the Federal Court of Canada or the superior court of a province, and members who are all judges of the Federal Court or of a superior district or county court of a province. For the convenience of applicants or beneficiaries who appeal at this level, the board is empowered to sit and hear appeals at any place or places in Canada. Further, although in many cases the evidence can well be submitted via a written brief or presentation, where the chairman feels the applicant should appear before the board for one reason or another, provision is made for payment of travelling and living expenses, including any loss of compensation, while attending.
Bill C-22, which received royal assent on November 27, 1974, and which came into force on January 1, 1975, contains a number of amendments to make the appeal system as flexible and accessible as possible. Those changes affecting the Pension Appeals Board include the following: payment of the legal expenses incurred by an applicant or beneficiary when the appeal against a review committee is launched by the minister; provision for a vice-chairman who, if the chairman is absent or incapacitated, has all the
January 29, 1976

powers and duties of the chairman; an increase in the size of the board from a maximum of six to a maximum of ten, to permit regional panels; the authority for someone to appeal on behalf of an incapacitated person, and more flexibility in the time for, and the granting of, leave to appeal. I should note that, while most of these changes were before the House at the time the hon. member tabled his bill, they were not proclaimed in force until January 1, 1975.
In this context, I should like to note that the Canada Pension Plan administration receives between 140,000 and
160,000	applications for benefits a year. In September, 1975, some 687,000 Canada Pension Plan benefits were paid. Of those benefits, more than 400,000 were retirement benefits about 46,000 were disability pensions and nearly 109,000 were widows' or widowers' pensions. In spite of this volume of cases handled by the Canada Pension Plan administration, of the 11,000 denials for benefits in the fiscal year 1974-75 only 1,800 requests for reconsideration were brought to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In the vast majority of these cases new information was brought forward. Consequently, in two-thirds, or 1,200, of these requests for review the minister decided in favour of the applicant or beneficiary.
Further, less than half of the remaining 600 appellants whose requests for reconsideration had been denied chose to pursue their case to the review committee stage. I am sure that all hon. members realize that this represents a very small proportion of the total volume of cases handled by the Canada Pension Plan administration on a yearly basis.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the very plausible case that the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) has made against Bill C-265, I still think that this House should lean over backwards, if it has to do that, and send this bill to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs so that it can be studied.
I was involved in the discussions and all the rest of the activity relating to the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan. I can confirm what the hon. member for Scarborough West has said about it. In fact, I welcome this opportunity to say again what a good plan it is. I shall have more to say about that in a moment. But surely even those of us who are friends and supporters of the Canada Pension Plan have the right to point out weaknesses if we feel there are any in it.
I need not review the whole course that the previous speaker outlined. May I emphasize the fact that the only way in which an applicant's case gets before a review committee is if that applicant feels he has been wronged. In no case does the minister or the department refer a case to a review committee. That happens only when an applicant for the pension feels that the bureaucracy has unfairly turned him down. It is something like going before an ombudsman. An applicant has the right, as we all know, to have a review committee established, and in certain cases the review committee does find in favour of the applicant.
Canada Pension Plan
Even after one has made the argument that the last speaker made about the need to have consistency of rulings because of the large numbers of cases involved, it makes a mockery of the right to go before a review committee if the minister then has the right to appeal the favourable decision of that committee and get the case thrown out.
If we need to have some concern about consistency of decisions, surely there can be some way to establish case law, or some way by regulation, to set limits surrounding these review committees. To repeat the words I have already used, it seems to make a mockery of the review committee structure if an applicant who gets a favourable decision is then turned down on the initiative of the minister. As I already said, it is like a person going before an ombudsman, asserting that the bureaucracy has done him wrong, getting the ombudsman to say that he is right, and then finding that Big Brother in the office of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has the right to take the matter one step further.
I realize that the applicant who has been turned down by the review committee has the same right, namely, to go to the Pension Appeals Board. However, what we are dealing with here is the case of the individual who feels that under the law he has the right to a pension for which he has paid. For him to feel that the cards are stacked against him in this way does lead to a feeling of grievance.
I am freely admitting a point made by the hon. member for Scarborough West, namely, that if you have a few hundred review committees coming up with different decisions there is going to be confusion as to what is right and what is wrong. However, that can surely be handled in some other way than this present arrangement which is built into the act and gives the Minister of National Health and Welfare the power to offset the favourable finding of a review committee.
I, too, welcome the fact that earlier in this session we passed an appropriate amendment to the Canada Pension Plan so that in this circumstance the applicant has his expenses paid. All told, however, I think the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), who brought in this bill, raises an important issue, one that concerns individuals, be they few in number. Because the case on its merit looks like one that is a real grievance, I hope the House will be willing to send this bill, or at least its subject matter, to the appropriate committee.
While I am on my feet there are a couple of other things I would like to say. I hope some day we can get behind this review committee procedure to the substance of the case to which the hon. member referred, namely, the restricted definition that applies to disability. The hon. member said that you need to have one foot in the grave and the other on a banana peel in order to qualify. I suggest it is just about that severe.
I suppose that most of us in our dealings with persons involved with Canada Pension Plan applications have many cases where individuals feel they are disabled. speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-265 which is before us this afternoon proposes to deny the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) the ability to appeal to the Pension Appeals Board a decision of a review committee under the Canada Pension Plan.
Any applicant for benefits or a beneficiary under the Canada Pension Plan who is dissatisfied with a decision regarding the level of or eligibility for CPP benefits may appeal the decision through three separate appeal stages.
At the first level, those who wish to do so may make a request to the minister for reconsideration of a decision taken by the CPP administration. In the last fiscal year some 1,800 such requests were made and of these 1,200, or two thirds, were decided in favour of the appellants. Some 97 per cent of these requests involved the determination of disability. In such cases additional evidence or altered circumstances may be brought forward, and, consequently, influence the application of the legislation.
In the same period 274 persons availed themselves of the opportunity to pursue their appeal to the second level of appeal, that is, the review committee. This represents fewer than half of the 600 ministerial reconsiderations which had been denied.
I should like to mention here that each review committee consists of three members, all of whom are Canadian residents. One of these members is to be appointed by the applicant or beneficiary and one is to be appointed on
(Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).]
behalf of the minister. These two members then jointly appoint a third board member to act as chairman. If the two members cannot agree on the choice of a chairman, the appointment of the chairman may be made by a judge of a superior, district or county court in the applicant or beneficiary's province of residence or, in the case of a non-resident, in the province in which the applicant or beneficiary's review committee member resides. The review committee hearing takes place in a location in Canada determined by the chairman with regard to the convenience of the applicant or beneficiary and the minister.
At the inception of the Canada Pension Plan the availability of this second level of appeal to a review committee was provided to avoid putting applicants and beneficiaries to the expense of a formal application to a court at the first stage of appealing the decision of the minister. Instead the appeal can be made to these locally constituted bodies. The accessibility of the appeal process was further broadened in the recent amendments made to the plan which came into effect on January 1, 1975. These provisions allow a third person to appeal a decision on behalf of an incapacitated applicant.
A decision of a review committee may be appealed to the Pension Appeals Board by the appellant or, again as recently amended, by someone acting on his or her behalf in certain circumstances. The opportunity to appeal a review committee decision to the Pension Appeals Board is also available to the minister. I should emphasize that an appeal by the minister is not necessarily presented in order to deny a benefit to a potential recipient. As an illustration, let us consider the case of two claimants-a legal and a common-law spouse-for survivors' benefits in respect of one contributor. Where a review committee decision awards the benefit to one survivor this effectively excludes the second surviving spouse both from the benefit and, more important, from an appeal of the decision itself. In this and similar circumstances the ministerial appeal to the Pension Appeals Board represents the interests of third parties affected by review committee rulings.
Beyond the implications of review committee decisions for parties affected by the specific case, the broader picture of equity and uniformity of legislative application between applicants and beneficiaries in similar circumstances is crucial.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when he was speaking a few minutes ago, suggested that this consistency or uniformity of rulings could perhaps be achieved in some other way. I would point out that the members of the review committee are not judges, they are not-

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext: They are human beings.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MINISTER'S RIGHT TO APPEAL DECISIONS OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are not people trained to handle judicial decisions of that type, so the first time a matter really comes before judges is when it goes to the Pension Appeals Board; that is the first time you have a body which is studying cases right across the country, so this is the advantage, at this level, of getting uniform decisions and a consistency in the rulings made.
January 29, 1976

The Canada Pension Plan is a complex piece of legislation, since it provides such a broad range of intended benefits. The program covers virtually the entire Canadian labour force outside of Quebec, and provides income security for contributors and their families. Obviously every possible individual circumstance cannot be anticipated and covered in the legislation, or its regulations, nor for the sake of flexibility should this be attempted. However, in providing for the discretionary application of legislative provisions, and appeals thereto, the possibility is ever present that a given interpretation of the legislation, which had been applied acceptably and uniformly, may be altered, reversed, or even completely disregarded in an isolated case of appeal to a review committee. In the interests of so many past, present, and future applicants or beneficiaries in similar circumstances, it is essential that such conflicting interpretations of the legislation be referred to a higher judicial body capable of rendering an informed and authoritative decision. The Pension Appeals Board, made up as it is of judges, provides such a forum.
It cannot be expected that an individual appellant will take upon him or herself the onus of establishing criteria by which to ensure the fair disposition of Canada Pension Plan benefit cases in general. This responsibility falls to the minister. If we conclude, and I believe we must, that such a judicial forum is essential to the proper administration of the Act, then by denying the minister access to the Pension Appeals Board I can only conclude that the hon. member is suggesting that such applications for judicial rulings must be made by the minister directly to a federal court.
In all of this the House can be assured that the position of the individual in such appeals is given much consideration and every effort is made to ensure that the applicant or beneficiary is not placed at a disadvantage. To this end a series of legislative amendments was implemented effective January 1, 1975, to improve the plan's appeal system. The first, to which I referred earlier, extends full rights of appeal to representatives of applicants or beneficiaries who are unable to act on their own behalf. A second amendment provides that in cases of ministerial appeal to the Pension Appeals Board, the affected applicant or beneficiary, or his representative, may be paid their legal expenses, thus ensuring their ability to be represented by counsel at such an appeal. Also, provision was made for the membership of the Pension Appeals Board to be expanded in order that cases might be heard more expeditiously and the position of the affected individuals not be prejudiced by lengthy delays.
With these amendments, difficulties to clients arising our of ministerial appeals have been ameliorated. In conclusion, it is important to retain the authorization in the legislation for ministerial appeals in order to ensure the continued effective administration of the Canada Pension Plan legislation.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, allow me to say that I am quite pleased to take part in this debate. I know that the legislation now under consideration is quite important, as indicated in the preface of a report entitled "A New Perspective" and signed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who states the following:
Good health is the bedrock on which social progress is built. A nation of healthy people can do those things that make life worthwhile, and as the level of health increases, so does the potential for happiness.
Since we are considering a bill amending the Medical Care Act, I have taken the liberty of quoting this paragraph clearly showing the importance of this legislation.
Like many other members, I have a lot of material on this matter. I do not intend to quote it word by word in this House, because, on the one hand, I have already read

the minister's speech relating a long history of this legislation dealing with medical care and shared costs between the federal government and the provinces. He referred also to the efforts made by the government for several years. I also checked the fine speech delivered by my colleague from Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), the opposition critic, who has tried in a fine manner to make the government aware of the weaknesses of the measure. Since other members have made speeches in this House, I retain a series of figures, analysis, all explaining the situation as it is. That is why I shall abstain from quoting all these statistics, although they are very serious and worthwhile, since they have already been recorded in this House.
As far as I am concerned, Madam Speaker, this legislation poses a substantial problem, in the sense that it affects in a very direct, very particular and very precise way, negotiations that must take place between the provinces and the federal government.
Last June, the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) announced that the government intended to reduce its participation in the cost of medical services. In this way, the federal government, in our opinion-and I think that Canadians agree-realized that the government, after forcing the provinces to participate in the medicare program a few years ago had decided by a legislation that the provinces which would not participate would lose millions. So, these provinces were naturally forced to "embark" on a program for which some of them were not ready yet. I must therefore say that there was a lack of consultation. Last June, the Minister of Finance, on behalf of his government, reversed his policy and announced that the government would eventually retire from that program, in view of the increases. We certainly are in an inflationary context, but we do not accept forcing those people to pay for medical care. They have all sorts of handicaps, and they absolutely need our protection.
The government has gone ahead without any preliminary consultations with the provinces, and this bears repeating since after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) had made his statement and taken his decision, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) felt obliged to tour Canada to meet the provincial ministers. Of course, the minister says he has met with the provincial ministers and discussed it with them. We are not denying that, but we know perfectly well that this has not been done prior to the decision being taken by the government, and each time we wonder why.
It is not the first time the provinces are not consulted appropriately. That is why I feel this is a basic problem. I would like to have a federalism of participation. We have a federalism where some provinces are complaining about this lack of consultations. Of course, some hon. members will say I am exaggerating. Yesterday my colleague from Athabasca quoted some statements by provincial ministers; that is the undeniable proof that several provinces are not satisfied and claiming better consultations.
For instance, I must say the situation was the same when there was talk of anti-inflationary measures, and again when the matter of taxing our natural resources was discussed, and more recently, when there was talk of setting up a federal park in the province of Quebec. It seems that consultations were sadly lacking. I have a feeling, Madam
Medical Care Act
Speaker, that you will bring me back to the subject at hand, but those are as many examples I want to mention to stress the fact that the lack of consultation is not something new; the time has come to remind the government of the importance of those consultations and the participation of the provinces. That is why I gave examples which, once again, taking into account the declarations of provincial ministers, prove that there is not enough consultation. And then people wonder why the provinces are disatisfied, why the government is becoming less popular, why it is losing some of its credibility at the present time.
And so, we, on this side of the House, believe that it is important that we should protect the quality of our health services; we also believe thoses services are necessary for those who need them; I wonder to what extent the government takes that into consideration when it speaks of dollars? The paragraph I read at the beginning is marvellous. It was signed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare; if that wonderful thought serves as a source of inspiration, one dares hope that the government will spare no effort to ensure essential cares to the Canadians who need them. We are told that there will be cuts especially in expected increases. Even a government member this afternoon was giving us the evidence that there would be increases. We do know that there will be some more, and it is sure that if the government lowers its contribution the poorest levels of the society, the poorest provinces will suffer more than the richest provinces. So, by foreseeing this unacceptable injustice to these Canadians, we are naturally and necessarily justified to oppose the passing of a piece of legislation which does not meet the needs of that just society promised in 1968.
In view of this dissatisfaction, of this refusal by the provinces of a possible agreement, the minister concluded that something had to be done, because the negotiations did not end the way he wished. Is it possible to talk about a viable federalism as long as the provinces will not be able to find a certain security? I do not think so. So, we believe in these negotiations. We favour a federalism of participation as well as a certain de-centralization. And we believe that Canadians are ever more inclined to reject that centralizing federalism.
I know that those words may seem harsh to some hon. members in this House but it is important that the public know that the government is asking us to pass a law which is not acceptable to the provinces and therefore to Canadians in all parts of the country. We believe it is our job and our responsibility to tell the government that we refuse to play the role they expect us to play and that we would rather assume our responsibilities which demand that we respect the provinces. Now this bill shows in practically every clause a disregard for provincial wishes; it does not square with the objective which a minister of health should set for himself or the government fulfill for all Canadians.
Madam Speaker, it is not my intention to quote statistics again. They have been mentioned. I simply wish to talk about this aspect of funding which is as always the battlefield, and about the lack of meaningful negotiation between the provinces and the federal government. It is not the first time, as I have said before. It is unfortunate and

alarming, and the government can wonder why there are so many objections and why it is now impossible to maintain a certain credibility; it is because they are far from meeting the solutions and recommendations put forward by the provinces. And we believe that the provinces have something to say in this particular field, because they always had important decisions to make as regards health care.
Nevertheless, it is the federal government which, some years ago, felt most generous when it agreed to pay 50 per cent without restrictions. But today, these medical costs are always increasing for all sorts of reasons, but not necessarily because of the provinces, and the same thing happens in every field, Madam Speaker. The federal government makes a decision-without negotiating, I repeat- and informs the provinces in advance. Once the decision is made, the provinces are consulted and put before the fait accompli. The government is in the habit of putting the provinces in a strait-jacket. After, they negotiate. In my opinion, this is fair.
That attitude on the part of the government vis-a-vis the provinces is sheer confrontation. It can only bring major problems. So, Madam Speaker, I think that the role of the opposition which sees in this legislation a lack of respect toward the provinces as well as an impossibility to achieve the objective that the minister set for himself in a particular brochure, necessarily forces him not only to inform the members of this House that this bill is unacceptable but that Canadians must know that we are trying today on their behalf to ask the government not to pass this bill until the ten provinces find valid reasons to accept it.
I think it would be indecent for a government to pass this bill without having the assurance of provincial participation. Madam Speaker, those are the few remarks I wanted to make in asking the members of this House to grasp the importance of respecting the provinces, to understand their arguments and allow them with the federal government to prepare a legislation that will offer possibilities of meeting objectives. It is important that this government supplement the efforts the provinces are making and become a coordinator of those efforts, taking into account the objectives of the provinces, instead of centralizing. That is the problem as it stands now. As often as legislation such as this is presented to us without the assurance of consultation and respect for the provinces, I think we have that role to play, that responsibility to ask the government to change its attitude, and I say to this government that the time has come for it to change its attitude and be mcuh more open to those negotiations.
Having said that, we would gladly support bills that are in accordance with the objectives the minister speaks about on paper but which cannot be met because of the approach he displays before this House.
Madam Speaker, I hope amendments will be brought in at the committee stage, that negotiations with the provinces will be respected and that this legislation will not be pushed further in this House until the ten provincial ministers of health agree with the minister sponsoring this legislation that is unacceptable to us at this point.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in introducing this bill the minister in fact, although he may seem to make some small concessions, proposes in a very fundamental way to implement changes in the method by which medical insurance costs have been paid for many years. The minister proposes that the cost of the programs, which substantially has been shared 50-50 by the federal and provincial governments, will now be handled in such a way that the percentage paid by the federal government in the coming years will be less, and probably substantially less than the 50 per cent which has been paid up until now.
In beginning his speech the minister had some very complimentary things to say about our system of health care and the way in which it is paid for. I think he has every right to be complimentary, particularly when we compare our system of paying for medical services and hospital services with the way in which such services are paid for in the United States.
Recently during the Christmas season a senior public servant, in the employment of the federal government, with his family visited a large city in the United States. One of his children became sick and had to be admitted to hospital. The family was told that the child would not be ' admitted to the hospital until they had first deposited a cheque in the amount of $1,500 with the hospital in order to take care of possible and probable hospital costs. It is a long time since any Canadian citizen had to face that kind of situation in this country, and we can thank the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who instituted the hospital insurance plan in Saskatchewan when he was premier, and the federal Conservative government which extended that plan to all the provinces in Canada, and also the federal Liberal government which, taking the example of the province of Saskatchewan, began a medical insurance plan paid for by the federal and provincial governments.
What the minister is proposing is what he first proposed in 1973, that is, that 50 per cent of the cost of medical insurance paid for by the federal government would no longer be paid but rather that on a declining scale the amount paid by the federal government would be capped, that a limit would be put on the increase paid by the federal government of 14 per cent in 1976-1977, of 10 per cent 1977-1978, and of a smaller amount, to be negotiated with the provinces, for future years.
No only do I disagree with the limit which the minister has put on for the next two years, I have a great deal of skepticism about the supposed negotiations and discussions which the government and the minister will have with the provinces. My skepticism is based not on supposition but on experience.
From the day on which the minister announced the limits on the amounts the federal government would pay every provincial government, all ten provincial governments, whether they be Liberal, Conservative or NDP- and I am certain the present Social Credit government of British Columbia will join the other nine provincial governments-objected, first of all to the federal government
January 29, 1976

refusing to pay 50 per cent of the cost as it has until now and, secondly, to the federal government deciding unilaterally that it would reduce the percentage which it paid.
Let us remember that many of the provinces ,did not want to become involved in a universal government sponsored, government operated medical insurance plan. If my memory serves me correctly, the province of Ontario with its Conservative government was the last province to join the medical insurance plan. They did not want to join that plan because they believed that the former voluntary plan was adequate and that all that a government should do is to pay the premiums for those people who cannot afford to be covered under the voluntary plans. So they did not join the medical insurance plan until the opposition parties started to point out to the electors of Ontario that they were losing hundreds of millions of dollars by not joining the plan. As a result, Ontario under a Conservative government was brought kicking and screaming into the national medical insurance plan organized and operated by the government.
The Government of Canada having persuaded, enticed, and browbeaten the provincial governments to come into the medical insurance plan, is now telling them that it is no longer prepared to pay for 50 per cent of the cost, that there is a limit on what it will pay next year, and that the ceiling will be lowered further in the years after that. That is a strange way for the federal government to act.
For almost 18 months the provincial governments have been trying to persuade the federal government and the minister to sit down with them and discuss what is wrong with the present plan and what could be done to limit the increases which are taking place. One would think, to listen to the minister and the government, that it is only the federal government that is concerned about the increase in the costs of medical insurance, and the next bill we will be discussing, I suppose, will be increasing the costs of hospital insurance. The provinces are just as concerned as is the federal government. Indeed I think it would be fair to say that the provinces are more concerned than the federal government because they do not have the ability which Ottawa has to raise money through taxes. What will happen?

No, they are not like wolves; they are not even in the wolf class. This bill has two purposes. One is to let the doctors continue to earn as much as they can, and the other is to get Ottawa off the hook.
The minister says we have one of the best systems of health care in the world. That may be true, but the fact is that Ottawa now pays only 50 per cent of the programs which it has unilaterally approved. The federal government does not pay for mental health care, public health programs, capital cost in the building of hospitals, and a host of other items.
Most of the provinces have inaugurated or plan to begin programs which are different from those which are now offered. They are programs which, if we can go on the experience of other countries, will probably be cheaper than the kinds of programs which Ottawa now funds such as expensive intensive care hospitals. Some of the provinces have gone into home care, or they are thinking of going into home care. Some have gone into dental care, optometric services, physiotherapy, and pharmacare. All these programs they have begun or are planning to begin, and they have to assume on the basis of what the federal government has said that they will have to fund them themselves.
By recognizing only approved costs for medical and hospital programs for cost sharing, Ottawa has encouraged the utilization of high cost services. I could go into detail with examples which I have personally come across where Ottawa funds very expensive services at the rate of 50 per cent and will not pay for cheaper, alternate costs which have not been approved in advance. Any province which has gone into alternative programs, or wants to go into such programs, will have to find all the money itself. In doing that it would probably lose federal financial contributions which it is now getting, even if the alternative programs were to reduce the costs of hospital and medical expenses.
The provinces have proposed alternatives to the present 50 per cent cost-sharing. They proposed that the federal government agree to cost-share on the 50-50 basis the total cost of provincial health expenses on a capital basis, or

continue the present arrangements but expand them to include payment by the federal government of 50 per cent of the cost of mental and tuberculosis hospitals.
In 1974 the provinces agreed to accept the federal government's financing proposals and to undertake a joint analysis to try to define more precisely those concerns which they had voiced in previous discussions with the minister and with the government. Their study showed that most provinces would experience a very serious shortfall in revenues under the GNP escalator plan compared to the present arrangement, even with the so-called risk sharing modifications which the minister suggested when he first brought forward these proposals.
Their study also showed that the "thrust funds" proposed by the minister would be barely adequate to cover the shortfall in some provinces, and far from sufficient to offset losses experienced in other provinces. The study provided for the first time a reasonably accurate summation of the probable future cost of existing provincial programs and of committed new programs which are cost sharable at the present time.
Most provinces in recent years have committed themselves to improve services and to bring about greater efficiencies through the introduction of new programs-despite the fact that these efforts were not supported by any cost-sharing assistance from the federal government. Now they realize they cannot afford to consider let alone accept a new financing formula which would give them even less assistance than they are receiving at present.
According to the joint provincial study the ten provinces are now spending a total of over $1.2 billion a year in respect of health programs for which there is no federal cost-sharing at the present time. They claim that by 197879 these expenditures will increase to almost $2 billion annually. In addition commitments have been made to spend over $800 million on new non-sharable programs between now and 1978-79.
Many provinces have come to the point where their options are becoming more and more limited. Already many are finding it necessary to impose stringent budgetary restraint to the detriment of existing operations in order to free funds for essential new programs so as to reduce costs in the long run. They will not be able to maintain this situation if their health needs are to continue to be well served.
They feel, and I believe that the federal government has a clear responsibility to see to it, that all Canadians are guaranteed continuing high health standards regardless of the region in which they live. They have argued that this responsibility requires that the Government of Canada make certain that its financial support for health programming takes into account the varying fiscal capacities of the provincial governments which must provide this health care.
It is precisely those provinces in the have-not areas which will be hit the hardest by the minister's proposal for reduction in the contribution made by the federal government.

The ten ministers of health, including Conservatives and the NDP, met in Ottawa on January 14 and 15, 1975, in connection with this particular proposal. They came to the following conclusions, which I should like to put on the record:
First, that each province should receive no less federal financial support than it would have received for the funding of health insurance programs under current arrangements;
Second, that new financing arrangements must allow the provinces flexibility to pursue programs in accordance with their own particular priorities;
Third, that new arrangements must allow for equitable cost-sharing of both the "start-up" and continuing operating costs of new programs, as well as changes within existing programs, and
Fourth, that new arrangements should relate to health goals and objectives and should provide encouragement to new provincial programs which offer alternatives to high cost services. Examples of such alternatives include home care, geriatric services, community, health services and ambulatory care.
They added:
-the provincial governments do not believe that current problems can be dealt with through arrangements which would impose an arbitrary and unrealistic limit on the federal government's future financial involvement in major national health programs. Proposals for that kind of financing system, with a number of minor variations, have been discussed for over four years, and they have been formally and finally rejected by the provinces.
Provincial administrations do not need an arithmetic ceiling on federal payments to guarantee that they will be responsible in program operations. The simple fact of federal-provincial fiscal imbalance ensures that it is more difficult for provinces to raise their share of any program costs than it is for the federal government to raise its share.
In any case, the federal government has a clear responsibility to share equitably in the costs of providing health care to all Canadians. This is the basic principle underlying the hospital insurance and medicare financing arrangements and it is a principle which must be maintained if high national service standards are to be preserved.
This principle, which was first enunciated by a Liberal federal government, is now being violated.
The province of Manitoba co-operated with the other provinces in the analysis of the problems of financing health care, and tried to define more precisely what many people have voiced in previous discussions with the federal government about the future of health care financing. Their studies showed that most provinces would experience a serious shortfall in revenues under the GNP escalator, which I already talked about and which they calculated. I have not seen any studies by the federal government to dispute the estimates. The $1,200 million which they will be spending next year on health care is not cost-shared by the federal government.
The provinces thought they were making some progress until the June, 1975, budget was introduced by the former minister of finance. A primary element of that budget was restraint. It was achieved to a large extent by the imposition of arbitrary, arithmetic limits on federal contributions toward medical care insurance starting in the 1976-77 year. The province of Manitoba called on the federal government to change this policy.
The Manitoba minister of health sent a telex message to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which he said, and I quote:

These announcements came as a major surprise to me, and I assume that most other provincial health ministers experienced the same reaction. Only a few months ago, at a federal-provincial conference of health ministers in Ottawa, you indicated:
(1)	That your government recognized provincial concerns about the inflexibility of existing health financing-arrangements;
(2)	That you had agreed to abandon an equally rigid plan for imposing arbitrary federal expenditure limits, and
(3)	That you were willing to explore with the provinces various alternatives for improving the cost effectiveness of our health programs within the context of a more flexible interpretation of existing federal legislation ...
Your government's decision to proceed with major financing changes on a unilateral basis is a serious disappointment to our province and, I assume, to most others-all of whom, in good faith, have been devoting a great deal of staff, time and effort to the joint study of cost saving alternatives. Not only does the decision represent an apparent breach of our earlier understanding but also, and more importantly, it suggests that your government has every intention of implementing legislative changes which will cause the primary financial responsibility for the future reform of health care and for the maintenance of existing service standards to be borne by the provincial governments and their taxpayers. Given the recognized limits of provincial budgetary capacities, it is obvious that such a decision would represent a significant threat to our national health standards-standards based on a system which the federal government itself initiated.
That was sent on June 25, 1975. The federal minister replied on July 11. He said in part, and I quote:
When the deputy ministers report to us in the fall, as requested at the January meeting of health ministers, it would be my intention to propose that we move on to another stage in our negotiations in terms of considering what should replace the existing legislation.
Despite the minister's promise implicit in that telegram that there would be further meetings with the provincial ministers, there have been no such meetings until this time. I ask the minister why is this? Why did he chicken-out of a meeting with the provincial ministers?
When the provincial health ministers met in Victoria in August, 1975, the Manitoba minister of health and social development prepared a number of questions which he felt would have to be discussed before the provinces could agree to the proposal of the federal government. I am not going to put all of them on the record. Some, however, are very important, and not just to the government but to the people of the provinces. They will have to meet the shortfall which will be created by this unilateral decision of the federal government to put a ceiling on the increase which it will pay. Let me put on record-

Madam Speaker, I wish to use all the time allotted me to discuss a very important bill now before us. It must however be realized that this bill is closely related to the overall government program to curb
January 29, 1976

inflation. I believe this should be stressed in this debate. Certainly there is no question of downgrading medical care, as has been suggested by opposition members. This is absolutely without foundation.
We must review the health program and find out how we can now reduce certain expenditures that are now becoming astronomical in the area of medical care and hospital care in Canada.
Opposition members do not seem to make serious efforts to closely scrutinize the need to reduce expenditures. We are now in an inflationary period and for the sake of this country's survival, strong measures must be taken to solve our main problem, inflation. It seems opposition members do not agree, they even urge us, as they have been doing every day and even today during the question period, they have been urging Treasury Board to increase expenditures, although we are now striving to reduce them. The bill now before us is aimed at reducing expenditures without however reducing the quality of medical care.
I wish to commend the minister for the discussions he has been conducting with the provinces for a number of years, and since he assumed responsibility for the portfolio of national health and welfare.
After a number of discussions, several in-depth studies have been made in various provinces and in the province of Quebec by the Nepveu-Castonguay commission. The conclusion is that our present system must be rationalized and made more efficient. We should put less emphasis on the more expensive services and concentrate on finding cheaper alternatives such as long term care clinics as well as ambulance services and look for a more integrated system in which all the components could ensure the level of required services at a reasonable price. This is exactly what the federal government is now trying to do.
It is looking for better efficiency in the provision of medical care services which Canadians need. It is also trying to set up standards in relation to some medical care services. Participaction represents a very important step in this field and applies to all Canadians. I think that the more we will be able to provide programs such as Participaction, the fewer medical care services will be needed in this country.
During the past five years and when the first agreement was reached with the provinces, it was agreed that the federal government would reserve the right to review some of the programs during a five year period. That is exactly what is happening today. We are now reviewing different programs and this did not come as a surprise to provincial governments since, on many occasions, the federal minister communicated with them. He also held many meetings and informed them that at the present time, expenditures seemed to become huge and it was therefore necessary to review this very important program which has nevertheless become very costly, not because one area or another faces excessive costs, but because, I think, even in this field, we are trying to live beyond our means.
What is important is to try and live within one's means. I hope that opposition members will allow the bill to get speedy passage so that in future we may apply more efficient and less costly formulas in this field, while we still enjoy the same quality in medical care services. It
Medical Care Act
seems that in Canada the quality of medical care is much higher than that provided in other countries.
Therefore, in no way are we going to deprive Canadians of medical services, but we are trying to review a program as we do with many other programs in relation to cuts in expenditures that must take place within the federal government. Some alternatives are being sought to make medical services more radically available while reducing their cost and improving their efficiency.
In this regard, it is important to mention that according to the present forecast the cost reduction programs should allow us to save about $1 billion in a five year period. Now, I feel that we should have the unanimous approval of this House if we can assure the same quality of care and at the same time, in a five year period, save $1 billion. And I do not see why the members of the opposition talk so much about it and take the federal government to task for the agreements that it has already made with the provincial governments.
Up to a point, the provincial governments have been spoiled by the federal government, and they should now act on their own and take their own responsibilities in all areas, and not only as concerns health. Of course, the federal government has a very important responsibility, that of redistributing wealth throughout the country, and this bill aims at redistributing wealth to the most needy provinces.
As we know, the action announced by the federal government is now causing many misconceptions. The population should know that there is no question of depriving them of medical services and that the government only wants to increase the effectiveness of medical services and to take the necessary action to improve these services so that the population of Quebec and of the whole country can make fuller use of these services, but at a price somewhat more reasonable than at the present time since, if prices continue to escalate at the present rate, all the provinces and Quebec in particular will probably have to raise their taxes to compensate higher medical costs.
We can no longer hope for economic growth to go on at the spectacular rate that we have witnessed since the Second World War. We must therefore now find a better way to use our resources and reduce wasteful spending. In the field of hospital and medical services, there now is wasteful spending as costs have increased astronomically since the implementation of what we call medicare. We should take the necessary action for the provinces to realize that the federal big brother cannot always cover their deficits and provide them with financial means to allow them to say afterwards to the population that everything is the fault of the government.
Everyone should assume his own responsibilities and the provincial governments have very important responsibilities in this area. This is why the minister has tried during the years that he has been responsible for this department, to negotiate agreements which could likely slow down these overly steep price climbs. Unfortunately no agreement could be reached in some areas. This is why the federal government must show some leadership and institute legislation which, on certain points, willl make the provinces more aware of the fact that they are also responsible for the health of their citizens. They must contribute

to their health as much as the federal government. Mr. Speaker, I must say I was intrigued by the partisan remarks of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc). Before I proceed with what I have to say this evening on Bill C-68, let me assure the hon. member for Laurier that this party is trying to take a rational view of this bill, though little contained in the thrust of the bill is rational. The hon. member speaks about federal taxes that would have to be increased. I ask the hon. member, what can the provinces do but increase their taxes when the bill becomes law? They will have no other option.
I would also ask the hon. member to explain what he means when he says the provinces are being spoilt. Does not the hon. member know precisely what happened in 1965 when Mr. Pearson, the then prime minister, thrust this whole program upon the provinces? It was not until 1970 and 1971 that all of the provinces of Canada were finally brought under the cover of the federal medicare scheme. The hon. member says the provinces were spoilt but he should know better. I suggest that he examine the history of the federal medicare program and the manner in which the provinces were sucked into it.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, may I now address myself specifically to Bill C-68. We must first realize that once again we see a confrontation between the federal government and the provinces. It is the same kind of confrontation that we saw when we dealt with the mining legislation and mining taxation. It is the same kind of confrontation that we see going on with Bill C-58 which will inevitably mean a confrontation with the United States. It is the same kind of confrontation that has documented historically the actions of this particular government: there is no dialogue with the provinces and there is no consultation. The word is "negotiation", and brother, what experts they are.
Let us look at the increasing costs of medical care. I suggest the costs of medical care have not increased; it is the costs of institutional care and institutional structures that have increased. What could have been done about these costs, Mr. Speaker? Let us take a look at inflation, which has contributed to costs generally. Inflation has not

contributed to the increased costs of medical care when one remembers the increase received by Ontario physicians last year. Is a 4 per cent increase inflationary?
What about the additional cost of building new hospitals, or extensions to existing facilities? There is a 12 per cent building materials tax which the government put into effect. This could have been removed, at least for the construction of hospitals and nursing homes, indeed for every kind of health care facility. But it was not. Then look at other costs, such as labour. Finally-I know this is a provincial responsibility-but what about the length of time it takes a province to decide whether or not to expand a facility or to build a hospital? At the present rate of inflation, if plans are laid before a government today, a year and a half later they get the O.K. and the cost has increased by perhaps $2 million. These costs are all reflected in provincial coffers. These are the kinds of costs we are talking about today, not the sort of costs referred to in the bill. This bill is incorrect in its basic assumption that the cost of medicare is the question we should address ourselves to; rather it is the cost of institutional care with which we should be concerned.
The government could have done something for the provinces through CMHC and preferential interest rates. That in itself might have been a plus and could have been of assistance to the provinces. In the field of medicine the minister has cut, or at least frozen-which means the same thing with today's rate of inflation-funds spent on medical research. The government has been spending large sums in other areas. It spent $500 million on one program and $200 million on another. Why, Mr. Speaker, $500 million is one third of the total federal medicare budget. The money could just as easily have been directed into this particular area instead of introducing this bill.
Why should the minister of health introduce Bill C-68? Why should he take the action he is taking with reference to medical research in Canada? Surely he and other people recognize that our researchers, when they get involved in a program, begin research work that may take three to five years, but when they are half way through the program, perhaps on the verge of an exciting development or discovery which will be to the benefit of mankind, and certainly to the benefit of Canadians, along comes the minister and chops them off at the bootstraps. Where do these people go? They go right across the line to the United States where they know they can get a dollar's pay for a dollar's work and where their services, their intelligence, and their skills will be recognized and appreciated. This is the brain drain all over again. We had it before, and it is starting again.
When I came into this House in 1974 I can recall very well the appeal to the minister from members on this side for two lousy million dollars for research. The minister kept the research community of Canada waiting at his door for month after month after month. The question was asked time after time where was this $2 million. Finally out of the goodness of his heart the minister found that $2 million. The way the government was spending money then I am sure it had $2 million in its hip pocket all along.
