Let me refer again to the limitations of this bill. The provinces' view of this bill is already a matter of record. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) laid out precisely how the provinces feel about this bill. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) also told us what the provinces think. Are these members wrong, and are all the provinces wrong?
I think I should quote from the minister's publication "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians". At page 5 we find this stated by the minister:
Good health is the bedrock on which social progress is built. A nation of healthy people can do those things that make life worthwhile, and as the level of health increases so does the potential for happiness.
That is simply a beautiful statement. Let us look at another statement by the then minister of national health and welfare made in this House in July, 1966, and perhaps the minister will remember his own words. He said:
Health is not a privilege tied to the state of one's bank account.
I should like to add that health is not a privilege that should be tied to the bank account of the state. We should remember how cutbacks can eventually lead to problems as they exist at present in the United States. Not too long ago I was talking to a friend of mine whose husband fell ill while in Hawaii. He was an American citizen, a retired postmaster. He subsequently died while in hospital in Hawaii, and the hospital bill amounted to some $60,000. Thank heavens that this man was not a Canadian. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) touched briefly on this situation.
As the federal government changes the rules of the ball game and increases the cost load of the provinces we will see, insidiously creeping into the whole structure, the need and demand for private health care schemes, and we all know what follows this sort of thing. We can call it Blue Cross or whatever you will, but it results in fat premiums, escalating costs of medical care, and extremely escalating costs of institutional care.
Surely there is some sensible balance that can be struck. A good balance already exists, namely, the one that the federal government is inflicting upon the provinces. The minister refers to this balance in respect of the costs as a 50-50 split between the federal government and the provinces. Let me point out that it is not 50-50 at all.
The federal government is not paying the administration cost of provincial medicare schemes. The federal government is not paying a percentage of the para-medical care such as osteopathy in the province of British Columbia, physiotherapy in the province of Alberta, pharmacare in other provinces, and chiropractic care in Quebec. The federal government is not paying a share of any of those costs, yet the minister likes to tell the people that there is in existence a 50-50 proposition. I know better, and the minister knows better, and it is time that the people knew better. We all know that this is not a one-way street for the provinces.
Let me speak about the concerns expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North regarding accelerating costs of medical care. That hon. member has quoted fancy figures covering high earnings and high salaries of members of the medical profession. The information is not secret. In the province of British Columbia you can obtain a copy of
Medical Care Act
the blue book which lays out very clearly the incomes of professionals.
Let me point out that when you think about the high income of physicians and the earning capacity of those men, let us say $300,000, you must remember that this is probably a group of five doctors in a clinic. That is likely the total earnings of that clinic, but it does not say anything about the cost of the blood laboratory, the x-ray laboratory, and the host of other services provided by that clinic. There is no mention of the high cost of these things when that hon. member talks about the high medical fees and the high earnings of medical doctors.
The hon. member has not referred to the overhead the physician has in his own office. The hon. member must think that nurses work for free, that drugs are free, that x-ray films are free, and that all the lab work done is done for nothing. Fortunately the public knows better than this. The hon. member is grossly unfair to the medical profession when he distorts the facts in that fashion. I hope the poor man never needs a doctor. I am almost a doctor and that is why I am qualified to speak on this bill.
I might refer to a couple of massive volumes called the Faulkes Report. There are some sound suggestions in that report which nearly gave members of the medical profession in British Columbia a minor hemorrhage. One message from that report came through loud and clear, and I am sure it is a message that was accepted by the medical profession of British Columbia and by members of other medical professions in other provinces who have taken the trouble to read it. That message related to the need for a broader scope and broader interpretation in respect of health care.
A committee of this House has spent some time considering the so-called battered child syndrome. Does this situation involve a provincial responsibility without any federal share in the cost of operating a central registry so that we know who these child abusers are and where these abuses are taking place? Is the federal government not responsible in some respects?
If the federal government is prepared to have its members of the standing committee listen to all this evidence with reference to the battered child syndrome, then it is or should be obvious that the federal government is about to work up the machinery and accept some responsibility, or at least take a federal posture with reference to this problem. It is a health cost. How will that be funded? Will some little bill be slipped into this House on a 50-50 basis to deal with the provinces, and then later on will the ball game be changed to the satisfaction of the federal government? Most likely.
The increased cost of medical care in remote areas is another matter which should be of concern. The provinces would like to address themselves to this problem. They would like to provide the services and some incentive to doctors to move into the remote areas, certainly into my riding and into the ridings of many other members. How will they do this when along comes the Minister of National Health and Welfare who changes the ball game, who changes the sharing agreements, loads the provinces with extra costs, increases the costs of the premium and the cost

January 29, 1976
Medical Care Act
to the taxpayer while decreasing the quality of medical care, and decreasing the spending the provincial governments will have at their disposal for the development of new health care delivery systems?
Those are the problems that will be created by this bill. It will have a direct effect on the provinces. That direct effect will be felt by the taxpayer. The hon. member for Laurier expressed some concern for the taxpayer in federal terms but completely forgot about the provincial terms. I ask what this bill will do for the morale of the professionals?
There will very likely be an increase in the cost of the plan. There will very likely be a deterrent fee. This may represent an increase in the taxation. Certainly given the rate of inflation introduced and promoted so effectively by the government, the provinces will be forced into that situation. What will happen when the provinces become involved in that bind and sit down with the doctors to talk about the 4 per cent increase, or the 8 per cent increase, or the catch-up?
Many of the provinces this year are faced with doctors who need to catch up, who have had no increase for some considerable time. I can tell you now that the provincial purse strings will have to be tightened considerably, and that this will lead to acrimony and bitterness in the exchanges at the bargaining table between the health representatives and the provincial authorities. I know whereof I speak. I went through that route in 1968. I know all about it. Do not kid me that it will not happen.
Now, let us go back to the Munro task force report of 1969. In commenting on the rapidly increasing cost of health care the minister at that time said:
The standards of health care now available can now be reduced ...
That surely must be one of the most astounding statements I have heard in a long time. Environmental concerns are only now opening up new areas of health concern. The minister in 1969 said we were reducing our standards because everybody is healthy. Now all of a sudden we are in a new ball game of environmental diseases. We have to determine how to treat mercury poisoning. We do not have any experts in that field in Canada. All of a sudden we are in the ball game of the Port Hope radiation syndrome. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) does not know anything about that, or what he does know he is not telling. What about the cost of that particular fiasco; who will pay the shot? Is that part of the new formula under Bill C-68?
We might look at the study in Trail, my home town. This is a study on blood and hair taken from children and the smelter workers, and indeed from men and women in all walks of life. There have been 1,800 blood samples taken. This is a three-year study. It will be two years down the line before we can finish this study to determine the content in the blood and hair of heavy metals such as lead, zinc, copper, bismuth, and antimony. It will be two years before this can be finished but suddenly we discovered that some genius in the Department of National Health and Welfare had cancelled the program.
I must congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare-I hope he is listening to me-for responding in a very sensitive way and correcting that blunder so that that

study can in fact be completed. I should like to thank him on behalf of the constituents of my riding, more particularly those who have given their blood, hair, sweat, and tears in the past two years.
These are new concerns, new diseases, and disorders which have been presented to us all of a sudden. We have these environmental disorders, diseases, and industrial problems. Can we agree with the minister when he says that health care services can now be reduced because we have reached the zenith? He also said in his second statement that taxes, premiums or deterrent fees can be raised even higher. That will now be inevitable.
I must say that in British Columbia, if not in any other province, the Social Credit government was adamant about not applying a deterrent fee. It felt it was inequitable, wrong and inappropriate. The New Democratic government, I am told, when asked about a deterrent fee responded in like terms. Neither party will accept the application of a deterrent fee.
How can the minister give people something, and then suddenly take it away? That will really be the net effect of this bill. It will not take medical care away from the people but it will either increase their tax contribution or they will have to pay a deterrent fee to their physician.
Who will it hit first? It will hit the sick people. Who are the sick people? They are the people in two classes, the pensioners and the poor, the very ones who can least afford a deterrent fee or increases in taxes. That is another reason why this bill is iniquitous. Surely again we can agree at least in part with the statement of the then minister in 1969 when he said:
Ways must be found to restrain the growth of cost increases through better operation of the health service structure now in existence.
How true. So why did the minister not do it? There was task force after task force. There were seven which made 377 specific recommendations on how to improve the health care delivery system in Canada. What did the government do? The government did not look at one of them. It introduced a whole new formula, sucked in the provinces and chopped them off at the pass.
It bears repeating that the cost of health care facilities has experienced a dramatic rise. This is due to inflation. The cost to cover the expense of medicare has decreased, not the cost of hospitals but the cost of medical care. This cost has decreased in proprotion to the GNP over the last few fiscal years. Bearing that fact in mind, how does the minister rationalize his decision to introduce Bill C-68? It is what we call inductive reasoning.
I would suggest, finally, that if costs rise above the proposed cost sharing limits which the minister has introduced, there are three situations which could and probably will arise. One of them is the draining of provincial reserves and resources or provincial revenues, or conversely, as I have said, increased provincial taxes in order to meet the daily demands of health, not to mention the abandonment of new, innovative health schemes.
Another option, increased premiums, as I have said, increases costs for pensioners and those who can least afford it. Who is in a position to afford it? What will
January 29, 1976

happen when we get into deterrent fees and increased premiums in the provinces? Labour will say to management that that is part of its bargaining. Labour will say it cannot afford to pay increased costs for medical care, and it will expect to add them to its extra benefits. Labour will bargain for that. That is more fuel with which to stoke the fires of inflation and to put down the poor and the pensioners.
This is a simple bill. It contains only three or four pages. It is relatively insignificant in size. All it does is say that the government will make some changes in percentages, but no one on the other side of the House has really bothered to give serious consideration to the net result in province after province. It will not be too bad for us in British Columbia, but what will it be like for those in the Mari times?

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Once again we see the erosion of co-operative federalism. Brother, I do not think hon. members opposite know what those words mean. The government's five year notice for its withdrawal from the present hospital insurance plan threatens both these principles and practices. In the last ten years, as I said before, there have been seven task forces with 377 separate recommendations, and all of them have struck out. I wonder how much it cost for those seven task force reports.
I wonder what the cost was to the taxpayer, and I wonder where those task force reports are now. Who ordered them? Hon. members opposite ordered them. Where are they, and can they be produced? They are down in the archives confined to that limbo of dust, never to appear again. Why bother referring to a task force report? Why bother referring to 377 specific recommendations which could do something to cut the cost of health care and provide an efficient system, when all the government has to do is introduce a simple four page bill? It takes a hell of a lot less work, and the ball game is changed for the provinces. That is a pretty sweet deal.
By putting ceilings on these statutes which are on the books the government is ensuring that an inflation it helped generate will continue to escalate, medical costs will increase, and taxpayers will suffer. The desired standards for health care simply cannot be maintained because of the inherent restrictions within this bill. The government is making a guarantee that if inflation escalates, medical care will escalate, taxation will escalate, and the standard of medical care will diminish.
Finally, what will the provinces do this year? They will make darn sure they plump up to the best of their ability the medicare cheque because they know that the formula for the next five years is based on this year, and it is in their best interests to make this year look really good. That sure as hell does not do anything about inflation or for the cost of medical care.
Contrary to the idea of the hon. member for Laurier, this bill is not going to have an easy passage through the House or through the committee. All hon. members of the opposition will do their utmost to oblige the government to amend this bill and to come up with something which makes a darn sight more sense, costs the taxpayer less, and is more favourable to the provinces, and to see that there is
Medical Care Act
no more confrontation on this bill, but some consultation and negotiation something which has been long overdue.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming on at this stage of the debate on Bill C-68 one is likely to be considerably repetitious in terms of what has been said already. Nonetheless there are a few points which I think should be made, and they may be somewhat different from what we have already heard.
I should like initially to commend the critic on the opposition side, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk), for the very fine and extensive summary he gave to the minister.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: The only problem with his presentation was that it was so comprehensive and so intensive that it makes it difficult for the rest of us to follow.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
I should refer briefly to the presentation of the minister when he led off this debate on second reading. He was indeed leading off the debate on Bill C-68, as was intended, but as I listened to his presentation I got the impression he was talking about something other than medical care services. I will admit that there was a certain element in his presentation which dealt with medical services, but by and large his whole emphasis was on the excessive cost of health care.
He really did not take the trouble to explain to the House and to the people of Canada that in actual fact there has been a reduction in the rate of increase of medical care but a real escalation in the cost of health care. Perhaps not intentionally, but I think the minister is misleading people to think that there has been a real escalation in the cost of medical care, which is not true.
Be that as it may, the minister and the government are attempting to suggest that the need for this bill rests on the marked increase in the cost of health care. Because this is the allegation, and because other speakers who followed the minister chose to use the same sort of reasoning, I too-and I apologize-will branch off on this tangent of talking about health care as well as medical care.
When considering this problem one has to go back in history a little, because one cannot understand what is happening here if one does not consider what happened in the past. I should probably start off back in the days of Mackenzie King. I think we have to give him credit, or otherwise, for having initiated the approach to social services which we now have. One has to admit there are many good points about the social services we have, but there are problems. In retrospect one can say that probably one of the biggest problems we have is that Mr. King in his wisdom or otherwise decided, unfortunately, that he would bite off a segment of service rather than a segment of people. That is to say, he chose to lay the emphasis on one particular service people in Canada needed and to provide that on a universal basis, rather than establish which people in society needed that particular service.

January 29, 1976
Medical Care Act
I was glad to read the other day in Hansard that the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) saw fit to criticize our government a little bit, and to suggest that probably the time had come for us to consider whether the universality concept is valid in this day and age, or whether we should be more dynamic and try to make changes more appropriate to the times. In this case we have to live with this because Mackenzie King started it for us a good many years ago.
Next I should like to note that when we talk in terms of health care we are dealing with two different bills. We have the bill amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and we find that about 60 per cent to 70 per cent of all health care expenditures come under that act. It is unfortunate that so much stress in this debate is laid on expenditures which amount to only about 20 per cent of the health care dollar, namely, expenses under the Medical Care Act.
I think we should take a look at the fact that the government has served notice now that it will back off on both hospital insurance and diagnostic services over the next five years, and of course it will do something more immediate by way of Bill C-68 to cut back in the immediate future, beginning this year on payments under the Medical Care Act. One has to chastize the government considerably, not a little bit, for this sort of action, because if one looks back over the history one is impressed with the fact that back in 1967 and 1968 the government was warned that it would have difficulty in the future if it insisted on going along the path it was following.
I should like to read an excerpt from the record of the debates in the Ontario legislature on February 1, 1967, when the premier of Ontario at that time, Mr. Robarts, said the following:
Medicare is a perfect example of the federal government introducing unilaterally a program which imposes heavy financial responsibilities on the provinces. It is a further example that these things must be done together and must be done jointly if the decision-making process is to have any meaning. Mr. Speaker, unilateral decision without consultation is no substitute for good federalism.
There is no doubt in my mind that what Mr. Robarts was saying about nine years ago is still true today, that we have the very same government adopting the same policy of ignoring federalism and going on its merry path in a unilateral direction with complete disregard for the rest of the country. One has to be impressed with this unilateral and arbitrary action on the part of the federal government at that time, and again now.
Since the minister announced the introduction of Bill C-68 we find the unique situation of ten provinces and ten medical associations in complete agreement with each other and in disagreement with the federal government. It strikes one as being a rather odd situation that the minister is unable to introduce a bill which would be satisfactory to at least some of the provinces and some of the medical associations.
One could go on to look at the historic past in order to set the stage for the present time. There is a rather interesting article which appeared as an editorial in the Toronto Telegram issue of November 18, 1967, relating to the Medical

Care Act which was proposed at that time. The editorial referred to the comments of Mr. Macnaughton, the then treasurer for Ontario. I quote from the editorial as follows:
Already about 95 per cent of Ontario people have some form of medical insurance coverage.
As Mr. Macnaughton has pointed out, Ontario has other priorities. Under the proposed federal medicare program, however, the province will be taxed for this plan, whether it joins or not. The funds thus collected would be applied to medicare in the other provinces.
This is regrettable. It means, simply, that if Ontario doesn't toe the line, it will be deprived of its share of the medicare costs.
By pursuing medicare, Ottawa is forcing some provinces-including Ontario-to spend hundreds of millions on a program that is not wanted, not needed or required. At the same time, however, Ottawa will not permit the province to use this money for other essential programs such as housing, education and welfare.
This kind of approach to a hard fiscal problem is difficult to understand, especially when its known that the federal Cabinet is divided on this issue. Mr. Sharp's appeal for belt-tightening and spending cutbacks is put into a difficult context by this attitude.
How can there be confidence in the government, and in its ability to make important decisions affecting the nation, when the Cabinet is of two minds on medicare?
The editorial concludes:
The faith of Canadians in the Government's capacity to govern has been shaken by its handling of medicare. If it cannot assume responsibility in fiscal matters, how can it in such vital fields as foreign affairs, defence, justice and trade?
We could read the same words now and agree that they apply equally well to this day and age in Ottawa. The same holds true that we still have a government which was so irresponsible as to introduce a plan against the wishes of the people of Canada back in 1967 and 1968, having forced the provinces to join. It is difficult to believe. One can cite other examples.
I should like to quote from an editorial in the Telegram issue of December 5, 1967, in which Mr. Macnaughton is quoted as saying the following:
"The budget statement suggests a determination to pursue this costly measure of social security in the face of a recognized need for a cutback in government spending".
He said this determination is "totally inconsistent with the federal government's concern for the inflationary pressures, which have been caused, in no small degree, by the growth in government expenditures."
"I find it difficult to see how the federal government will be able to make an effective appeal for restraints on prices and costs by the private sector of the economy if it insists upon increasing the pressures from the public area", Mr. Macnaughton said.
Once again the same problem which existed eight years ago is with us today. Yet we wonder why we are having difficulty with the government and with this kind of legislation.
There is a very well publicised medical journal in Canada called Medical Post. I know the minister is familiar with it because not too long ago he wrote a letter to it. However, may I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and continue my comments tomorrow if this meets with your approval?
January 29, 1976

subtopic: ENERGY-POSSIBLE MEASURES TO PREVENT INCREASE IN COST OF OIL USED BY ATLANTIC PROVINCES TO GENERATE ELECTRICITY
ENERGY-POSSIBLE MEASURES TO PREVENT INCREASE IN COST OF OIL USED BY ATLANTIC PROVINCES TO GENERATE ELECTRICITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the facts of life so far as power production from Nova Scotia is concerned are that we have an oil based electrical system. In fact about 70 per cent of our thermal plants are fueled by oil, and the rest by coal. Many people ask why we do not use our coal for 70 per cent and oil for 30 per cent, but it is not that easy although it might appear so on the surface.
This week we were gladdened by the announcement that a new coal fired generating plant initially producing 150,000 kilowatts would be built in Cape Breton and brought into production by 1979. That is good news, even though it does not mean that the announcement of a new mine will be needed now to produce this power, but hopefully it will lead to the establishment of a new mine for the Nova Scotia thermal market by the early 1980's. Further we have reason to hope that an additional mine opening may be announced in early 1977-after the results of a new coal preparation and desulphurization plant are known.
Coal offers some short term relief for the province of Nova Scotia, but as the president of that province's power commission noted at the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council seminar on January 21 there is no certainty at the moment that more than 1,500,000 tons per year of new coal can be provided. Therefore it is unlikely, based on present available information, that Nova Scotia coal can take us beyond 1983 to 1984.
There is no time, Mr. Speaker, to go into the complex details of why we cannot project more coal for thermal power purposes in Nova Scotia other than the above figures because it relates to the price and availability of coal as against competitive fuel. The availability of Cape Breton coal is tied not only to the financing of future openings but also to the necessity of guaranteeing future coking coal requirements for a proposed new steel mill in Cape Breton.
What I am trying to say is that even with the interim help given to the province by using Cape Breton coal, and thus reducing to some extent our present dependency on foreign oil, for the next eight to ten years we will be still heavily dependent on oil.
In the rest of the country, with the exception of Alberta and possibly Saskatchewan, oil price increases have a very serious effect. They usually mean higher gasoline prices, additional home heating costs and, in the final analysis, higher prices for many of our manufactured goods and some of our service industries. But in the maritimes, and especially for Nova Scotia, they mean higher electricity
Adjournment Debate
prices. Nova Scotia is always harder hit because of its industrial capacity. Regions of it, like my own constituency with a large number of pensioners on relatively fixed incomes, are particularly burdened with home heating and power costs.
Last June the $1.50 per barrel increase for crude oil was a hard blow for us. If we are to be hit with another increase of $2 at the end of June it will be a catastrophe.
In answering the question of my concern regarding power costs in Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region that they could possibly be doubled from about 18 mills per kilowatt hour to 37 mills by 1980, and this was based on a conservative projected oil cost of $12.19 per barrel, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) replied by alluding to the help already given to the Atlantic region's power requirements by past subsidies and a repayable loan to the nuclear power station being built at Point Lepreau in New Brunswick. We are grateful for this help and for the recent indication of federal support for the development of the eastern Canadian power grid to improve the limited existing ties. The federal government has offered to pay 50 per cent of inter-regional transmission line construction costs. This is helpful, but it is insufficient given the size of the problem that we are going to face by 1980 as described by the speakers at the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council conference to which I have referred.
I suggested in the House on Monday that a rethinking of the subsidy arrangements had to be done immediately, and I am awaiting to hear from the minister's parliamentary secretary that this department and the federal cabinet are truly aware of the potential crisis facing us in a few short years. The minister and the cabinet have to realize that only four years ago the electrical power rates in Nova Scotia were about on a par with Ontario's; today they are double the national average, and could triple or quadruple that average by 1978 unless the federal government takes decisive action this year.

subtopic: ENERGY-POSSIBLE MEASURES TO PREVENT INCREASE IN COST OF OIL USED BY ATLANTIC PROVINCES TO GENERATE ELECTRICITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to respond to the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) on his concern regarding the oil price in the maritimes and the fact that a great deal of the power, especially in Nova Scotia, is generated from imported crude oil.
The government does not underestimate the effect of oil price levels on the price of electricity in the eastern provinces. This is why oil price cushioning was introduced to allow a period of transition and adjustment toward the world price of oil.
The hon. member's arithmetic on the effect of oil prices on electrical energy generation requires some clarification. The present cushioning on heavy fuel oil is slightly over $3 per a barrel. If this amount were eliminated immediately the resulting increase in oil fired generation costs would be about five mills per kilowatt hour. Estimation of price levels in 1980 involves many other factors which go well beyond the oil import subsidy and include considerations of rising capital costs and other operating costs, and of course the possible changes in the world price of oil.
211 30-41

January 29, 1976
Adjournment Debate
As my minister has pointed out, the government has encouraged the development of nuclear generation at Point Lepreau and has offered to support regional electrical interconnections to give greater flexibility and lower real cost in the provision of future supplies of electricity. I might point out that this offer of half of the cost of the nuclear generating station and interprovincial interconnections has been available to the province for quite some time. The cable inter-connection between New Brunswick and P.E.I. is a current example of the application of this policy with the aid of federal grants and loans.
In the longer term, a key factor is a close degree of co-operation between electric utility and government organizations in the Atlantic region, and I am somewhat encouraged by the studies presently being undertaken jointly by Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.

subtopic: SPORTS-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO AID FOR AMATEUR HOCKEY
SPORTS-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO AID FOR AMATEUR HOCKEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon during question period I attempted to find out from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) whether or not he shares his concern for amateur sport in this country as he did so effectively with his intervention in professional football in Canada, namely, the CFL. In my question I specifically referred to major junior hockey in particular and amateur hockey in general.
I had hoped that the minister would refer to the difficulties being encountered by many junior teams in different communities across this country, difficulties that they are encountering as a result of the delay and in some cases non-payment of development fees by the professional hockey leagues, specifically the World Hockey Association. I should not have been surprised when his answer was vague and uninformative.
I tried to be recognized to ask a more specific supplementary question of the minister, but for some reason Mr. Speaker saw fit not to allow me this common practice. Perhaps Mr. Speaker shares the same view as the minister in that professional teams rate more concern than our youth. That is certainly not the view that I take.
Be that as it may, the fact of the matter is that amateur sport falls under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare and, therefore, it would be only natural to assume that the minister in question would be interested in the well-being of the thousands of young hockey players in the junior leagues across the country.
In any case, what I wanted to find out this afternoon was whether the minister was aware that there exists a very strong possibility of some major junior hockey teams being in financial jeopardy primarily as a result of non-payment of development fees by the professional leagues.
The reason I raise this is because the federal government intervened in professional football. Under the circumstances I feel that it is time it should interfere in the case of these youngsters across this nation.
Allow me to remind the minister that in 1974 there in fact existed a contract between the CAHA and the NHL regarding development fees which amounted to nearly $2
[Mr. Foster.)
million in that year alone. Such a contract has not been renewed; subsequently most payments have ceased and junior hockey is finding itself in serious financial trouble. There are 34 teams, for example, in the major Junior A league and one can check with most of them, whether it be Sault Ste. Marie, Peterborough, Flin-Flon or others, and one will see this problem. Let us remember, the participants are all Canadians, not like the CFL teams where most of the coaches, management, and players are Americans.
One would think that, if the minister is interested in physical fitness and sports at all, his interests would be geared to the thousands and thousands of youngsters across this country rather than a few hardened professionals. However, the more one looks at the minister's record in this regard the more one sees that the minister's concern is indeed very minimal if not non-existent.
You need only to look at the tragedy in Montreal as it relates to amateur athletes, not only from our own country but from around the world. What a disgrace and embarrassment for this nation to have a $1 billion Olympic Games and not be in a position to provide adequate facilities to the youngsters from around the world. One billion, yet there are no flush toilets, showers, or other adequate facilities! Yet the minister, as head of the Quebec Liberal caucus and as the one responsible for amateur athletics, sits here and not only does he allow the situation to develop but he is one of the main backers of the team of mismanagers in COJO in Montreal which has brought embarrassment and shame not only to the minister's own province but to the rest of Canada as well.
It seems to me that either the minister does not care enough about our youth who forfeit a great part of their teen-age years for the sake of physical excellence or, if I may borrow a term from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), he doesn't know his razzmatazz from a hole in the ground when it comes to physical fitness and sports in this country. This was evident from the fact that when he was pushing his football legislation before the House he had to hire special speech writers for thousands of dollars because he obviously had no knowledge of the subject matter himself.
In any case, the question is simply this: based on the fact that the minister saw fit to intervene in professional football, is he prepared to intervene today on behalf of tens of thousands of youngsters in amateur athletics?
I believe the time has come for the minister to show his concern, whether it be to ensure that development fee payments are made by professional teams and leagues or to ensure, in his capacity as Minister of Health, that proper and adequate sanitary facilities are provided at the Olympic Games in Montreal or, in general, to ensure that in any sport where professional and business oriented corporations draw on the talents of our youth-talents which were partially developed as a result of federal financing-the development payments will be funnelled back to the grass roots of the various physical fitness institutions and programs. subtopic: SPORTS-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO AID FOR AMATEUR HOCKEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) described his question as a simple one. Indeed it is a simple one and I am glad to have an opportunity to clear the air. Let me say at the outset that all the allegations he has made against the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and against the government of lack of concern are based on a misunderstanding of the situation.
I shall not attempt to defend Mr. Speaker against the allegations the hon. member made against him at the beginning of his remarks. I am sure the Speaker is well able to defend himself in the proper way. But I reject the statement he has made about the government.
First of all, we certainly favour financial support for amateur hockey by professional hockey. In fact we have intervened several times in the past, and if the hon. member knows anything about amateur sport, as he certainly should, he would be well aware of this. We are prepared to intervene, and we have intervened. We have proven our interest in the past.
Adjournment Debate
Moreover, we are watching the situation very closely and we are well aware of what is going on. We are aware of the non-payments. We are aware of the allegations of delayed payments. We are acquainted with the status of those payments. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association is very well aware of our interest and our support. They know perfectly well that they can come to us and ask the minister to intervene. But here are the facts: we understand from all the parties that the climate of negotiation and the relationship between the amateur organizations and the professional organizations are improving. They are approaching a resolution of their difficulties on their own and therefore we do not intend to take any action at this time.
As far as we know, it is the view of all the parties, professional and amateur, that we ought not to intervene at this time. For the hon. member to say there is a serious problem-which we concede there is-but that we ought to intervene to solve it, is just grandstanding. We are ready to intervene if any one of the parties asks us to do so, and we would be prepared to do so as we have in the past. So much for allegations of lack of interest.
The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley made a very interesting suggestion and I also want to react to it on behalf of the government. He pointed out there are amateur and professional associations in other sports-he referred to figure skating-that have a relationship whereby the professional sport benefits from the training and practice provided by the amateur sports. He is right, professional sports do benefit from the amateur sports. If any of them on either side are prepared to take the kind of initiatives that have been taken in the field of hockey, we would certainly be prepared to support them. But we are not going to jump in on top. We are watching and are prepared to be supportive, and we have proved our interest and preparedness to be supportive. But we have no intention of jumping in on top of the amateur associations without invitation or an expression of interest on their part.
